title: What Companies Actually Mean When They Say They Want “AI Experience”
abstract: What Companies Actually Mean When They Say They Want “AI Experience” What employers actually mean when job postings list "AI experience" as a requirement. By Vinod Chugani on October 23, 2026 in Career Advice Job postings for data analysts, statisticians, and researchers increasingly list "AI experience" as a requirement. But that phrase means very different things depending on who wrote the listing, what industry they're in, and what problem they're trying to solve. A hiring manager at a retail company, a biotech startup, and a financial services firm may all use the same two words to describe wildly different expectations. This guide breaks down what employers are actually asking for, how to read between the lines of job postings, and how your existing statistical knowledge maps onto what they call "AI experience." The Phrase Has No Standard Definition "AI experience" is a marketing term, not a technical one. Unlike "five years of regression analysis" or "proficiency in R," it carries no shared meaning across organizations. This ambiguity isn't an accident. Hiring teams often don't fully agree internally on what they want. They write "AI experience" because it signals modernity and filters for candidates who've been paying attention to recent developments — not because they have a precise competency in mind. Your first job is to decode the listing. The job description itself, the industry context, and the seniority level all carry information that tells you what the company actually needs. The 4 Categories of "AI Experience" Most uses of "AI experience" in job postings fall into four distinct categories. Understanding which one applies to a given role changes how you should frame your background. Category 1: Familiarity with AI Tools. This is the most common meaning at the entry and mid-level, especially in industries that have recently adopted AI products but don't build them. A marketing analyst role asking for "AI experience" often means they want someone comfortable using tools like automated forecasting dashboards, AI-assisted reporting platforms, or large language model (LLM) interfaces for summarization and drafting. They're not asking you to build anything. They want to know you can evaluate AI outputs with statistical judgment and fold them into existing workflows. If you've used any AI-assisted tool professionally and didn't just trust it blindly, this category applies to you. Category 2: Machine Learning Awareness. You'll see this most in tech-adjacent analyst roles. Companies want people who understand the difference between a classification problem and a regression problem, can read a model performance report, and can hold a coherent conversation with the data science team building the models. Note what this isn't asking: it's not asking you to build anything. If you understand concepts like training and test sets, overfitting, and feature importance, you qualify — even without hands-on modeling experience. Category 3: Applied Machine Learning. This is what most people assume every "AI experience" requirement means. It's also far less common than the phrase suggests. Roles that genuinely require this are usually titled Data Scientist, Machine Learning Engineer, or Applied Scientist, and they'll say so explicitly in the job description body, not just in a bulleted requirement. Look for language like "experience building predictive models," "familiarity with scikit-learn ," or "experience deploying models to production." If the listing just says "AI experience" in a bullet with no further detail, it almost certainly means Category 1 or 2. Category 4: Domain-Specific AI Knowledge. In specialized fields, "AI experience" refers to AI applications specific to that domain. Healthcare companies may mean clinical natural language processing (NLP) or imaging analysis pipelines. Legal firms may mean contract review automation. Financial companies may mean fraud detection frameworks or algorithmic trading systems. This is the easiest category to identify because the surrounding job description makes the domain explicit. If you have deep domain experience — even without broad "AI" credentials — this is where your background matters most. How Your Statistical Background Already Maps to AI Experience Statistical training is the foundation of almost everything called "AI" in a business context. The gap between "statistician" and "AI practitioner" is largely one of vocabulary and tooling, not underlying reasoning. You don't need to overhaul your resume. You need to translate it: Variance, bias, and model fit map directly to understanding why machine learning models fail. Regression analysis maps cleanly to how most supervised learning algorithms work conceptually. Hypothesis testing and experimental design are exactly the skills companies need when they want someone to evaluate whether an AI system is actually performing as expected. Where your resume says "built predictive regression models to forecast quarterly demand," a hiring manager reading for AI experience sees someone who understands supervised learning and model evaluation. Frame your experience around outcomes and reasoning processes, and the connection becomes visible. Reading the Job Posting as a Statistical Document Treat a job posting the way you'd treat any dataset: with healthy skepticism and a focus on what the evidence actually supports. Headline requirements are aspirational. Companies list every skill they'd ideally want, knowing no single candidate will check every box. "AI experience" buried in a list of twelve requirements carries far less weight than you might think. What carries more weight is what appears in the role description body — the day-to-day responsibilities and the problems the role is supposed to solve. A useful shortcut: If the responsibilities involve analyzing business performance, presenting findings to stakeholders, and supporting strategic decisions with data, it's an analytics role with AI awareness requirements (Categories 1 or 2). If the responsibilities involve designing, training, evaluating, and deploying models, it's a true machine learning role (Category 3). The headline requirements often fail to communicate this distinction clearly. The body of the posting usually does. Also pay attention to the modifiers. "AI experience preferred " is a nice-to-have. "AI experience required " with no further elaboration usually means Category 1 or 2. "Hands-on machine learning experience required" with specific tools listed means Category 3. The Seniority Signal The seniority level of a role changes the interpretation of "AI experience" substantially. Seniority Level What They Actually Want What That Looks Like in Practice Junior Adaptability Comfort with new tools, willingness to learn internal systems, no fear of AI outputs Mid-Level Informed Collaboration Working alongside engineering teams, contributing to model evaluation conversations, bridging the gap between data science and business stakeholders Senior Strategic Judgment Knowing when AI is and isn't the right solution, communicating limitations to leadership, helping the org avoid the real costs of deploying it carelessly Three Misconceptions Worth Clearing Up "I should list every AI tool I've ever touched." This tends to backfire. Hiring managers remember candidates who demonstrated judgment, not candidates who demonstrated access to tools. Describe the problems you solved and the reasoning process you used, then mention tools as supporting context. "I'm disqualified if I haven't built a machine learning model from scratch." For the majority of roles using this phrase, you're not. What actually disqualifies candidates more often is an inability to think critically about data quality, model assumptions, and result interpretation. Those are statistical skills — and they're exactly what companies need but often fail to name correctly in their postings. "I need a certification before I apply.

title: 5 Free AI Coding Agents You Should Try in 2026
abstract: 5 Free AI Coding Agents You Should Try in 2026 Access powerful open-source and proprietary models through OpenCode Zen, Gemini’s free quota, Kilo Gateway, Cline Provider, and Charm Hyper without paying for API access upfront. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on October 23, 2026 in Programming AI coding agents are no longer just for companies or developers willing to pay for expensive APIs. Even without a credit card, you can now try capable agents powered by the latest open-source and proprietary models from Google and other AI labs. These agents can inspect repositories, edit files, run terminal commands, debug errors, execute tests, and work through complete coding tasks. That is one of the best parts of the current AI revolution: a lot of this technology is already accessible if you know which tools to use. The problem is that many coding agents still require a paid subscription or API key before you can properly try them. This guide focuses on tools that give you a practical way to experience agentic coding and test strong models without paying for API access upfront . Coding Agent Free Model Access Best For OpenCode OpenCode Zen free models Best overall Gemini CLI Gemini free quota Best free allowance Kilo Code Kilo Gateway free models Best variety of free models Cline Cline Provider free models Best for IDE users Crush Charm Hyper free tier Best terminal experience 1. OpenCode OpenCode is one of my favorite open-source coding agents, and I use it almost every day. It gives you a terminal-based coding environment where the agent can explore your repository, edit files, run commands, and handle multi-step development tasks. One of the main reasons I keep coming back to it is OpenCode Zen . If I want to test a newly released model, there is often a free option available through Zen, so I can try it directly inside my coding workflow without setting up another provider or paying for API credits. And these are not necessarily small or low-quality models. OpenCode regularly provides access to capable models for free, including variants from Muse Spark, Ling, NVIDIA Nemotron, and experimental or promotional releases. The exact free catalog changes over time, which also makes Zen a useful place to experiment with new models as they become available. You mainly need an OpenCode Zen account to get started with these free models. 2. Gemini CLI Gemini CLI is Google's open-source terminal coding agent. It can understand repositories, modify files, run shell commands, use tools, and work through multi-step coding tasks directly from your terminal. Google is probably one of the most generous model providers when it comes to free access. With Gemini CLI, you don't need to buy API credits or configure a separate model provider. You can simply install the CLI, sign in with an eligible Google account, and start using Google's latest Gemini models. There is an important limitation, though: free access is still rate- and quota-limited . It is great for testing, learning, and smaller coding tasks, but I wouldn't rely on the free tier for heavy, continuous development on large real-world projects. 3. Kilo Code Kilo Code started as a VS Code coding agent, but it has grown into a much broader ecosystem. You can now use it through VS Code, JetBrains, the CLI, and Kilo's cloud services , giving you much more flexibility in how you work. It also supports hundreds of models, so you are not locked into a single provider. The best part for me is its selection of free hosted models . Kilo regularly offers capable models at zero inference cost, and you can simply search for free in the model picker to see what is currently available. The exact selection changes as providers and promotions change, and some models may have upstream rate limits. Even better is Auto Free ( kilo-auto/free ) . Instead of choosing a model yourself, Kilo automatically routes your requests to one of the best free models currently available, with no credits required. That makes Kilo especially useful if you want to experiment with different modern coding models without constantly checking which free option is available. 4. Cline Cline is another coding agent I really like, especially if you prefer working directly inside your IDE. It can inspect your codebase, create and modify files, run terminal commands, check errors, run tests, and keep iterating on a task until it reaches a working result. Cline also gives you a lot of visibility into what the agent is doing, so you can review actions before allowing it to make important changes. What makes it interesting for free users is that Cline regularly provides free models through the Cline Provider . Once you sign in, you can open the model selector and look for models marked FREE . These options change over time and usually come with usage limits, but they are a great way to test new models, learn how Cline works, and experiment with agentic coding without immediately paying for API credits. 5. Crush Crush is one of my favorite options if you enjoy coding directly from the terminal. It is built by Charm, the team behind tools such as Bubble Tea and Gum, so the terminal experience is extremely polished. At the same time, it is a proper coding agent with support for file editing, terminal commands, LSP integration, MCP servers, and multi-step coding tasks. The best part is Charm Hyper , Crush's own model provider. Hyper has a free tier, so you can simply install Crush, select a Hyper model, sign in, and start coding without setting up API keys or buying credits. The free plan currently gives you 100 Hypercredits every month , which makes it useful for testing Crush and trying some of its coding-focused models for free. Which One Should You Use? If I were starting today, I would probably try OpenCode first . It gives you a really good balance of agent capabilities, model flexibility, and free access through OpenCode Zen. After that, it depends on how you like to work. Choose Gemini CLI if you want the easiest access to Google's Gemini models, Kilo Code if you want a large selection of free hosted models, Cline if you prefer working inside an IDE, and Crush if you want a polished terminal-first experience. Of course, free models come with limits. Quotas can change, promotional models may disappear, and they may not be enough for heavy work on large production repositories. But that is not really the point. You can now install a capable coding agent, connect it to a free hosted model, and start experimenting with agentic software development without paying upfront. Abid Ali Awan ( @1abidaliawan ) is a certified data scientist professional who loves building machine learning models. Currently, he is focusing on content creation and writing technical blogs on machine learning and data science technologies. Abid holds a Master's degree in technology management and a bachelor's degree in telecommunication engineering. His vision is to build an AI product using a graph neural network for students struggling with mental illness. <= Previous post Next post =>

title: How to Process Large JSON Files in Python With ijson
abstract: How to Process Large JSON Files in Python With ijson I loaded a large JSON file in Python and watched memory jump from 43 MB to 808 MB. Here’s what happened and how streaming changed everything. By Kanwal Mehreen , KDnuggets Technical Editor & Content Specialist on October 22, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence JSON is one of the most common formats for storing and exchanging data in Python applications. For small files, Python's built-in json module works perfectly well: import json with open("data.json") as f: data = json.load(f) The problem starts when the file becomes large. json.load() parses the entire JSON document and creates the corresponding Python objects in memory before you can start processing the data. A file that occupies a few hundred megabytes on disk can therefore require much more memory once converted into Python dictionaries, lists, strings, and numbers. A better option for this type of workload is ijson , an iterative JSON parser that lets you process data incrementally. In this tutorial, we will use a large JSON file containing San Francisco land-parcel data. We will first process it with json.load() , measure what happens to memory, and then solve the same task with ijson . Step 1: Downloading a Large JSON Dataset For this experiment, we will use the San Francisco City Lots dataset. I am using Google Colab for this article. Download it using: curl -L \ https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zemirco/sf-city-lots-json/master/citylots.json \ -o citylots.json You can check its size with: ls -lh citylots.json The dataset is 181 MB in size, making it large enough to demonstrate the difference between loading and streaming JSON. The file follows the standard GeoJSON FeatureCollection structure. You can check it using this code: import json with open("citylots.json", "r") as f: data = json.load(f) print(data.keys()) data["features"][0] Output: dict_keys(['type', 'features']) {'type': 'Feature', 'properties': {'MAPBLKLOT': '0001001', 'BLKLOT': '0001001', 'BLOCK_NUM': '0001', 'LOT_NUM': '001', 'FROM_ST': '0', 'TO_ST': '0', 'STREET': 'UNKNOWN', 'ST_TYPE': None, 'ODD_EVEN': 'E'}, 'geometry': {'type': 'Polygon', 'coordinates': [[[-122.42200352825247, 37.80848009696725, 0.0], [-122.42207601332528, 37.808835019815085, 0.0], [-122.42110217434863, 37.808803534992904, 0.0], [-122.42106256906727, 37.80860105681815, 0.0], [-122.42200352825247, 37.80848009696725, 0.0]]]}} The important part for us is the features array. Each feature represents one parcel and contains two main sections: feature ├── properties │ ├── BLKLOT │ ├── BLOCK_NUM │ ├── LOT_NUM │ └── STREET │ └── geometry └── coordinates Our analysis only needs a few values under properties . However, if we use the standard JSON parser, Python still has to load all of the geometry coordinates as well. Step 2: Processing the File With json.load() Let's first use the approach most Python developers would naturally try. Create a file called standard_json.py : import json import time start = time.perf_counter() with open("citylots.json", "r") as f: data = json.load(f) features = data["features"] market_count = 0 first_five = [] for feature in features: properties = feature["properties"] if properties.get("STREET") == "MARKET": market_count += 1 if len(first_five) < 5: first_five.append( properties.get("BLKLOT") ) elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start print(f"Total parcels: {len(features):,}") print(f"Market Street parcels: {market_count:,}") print(f"First five parcel IDs: {first_five}") print(f"Time: {elapsed:.2f} seconds") The code is simple and perfectly valid. The problem is this line: data = json.load(f) Before our loop can process even one parcel, Python has to: Read the complete file ↓ Parse every JSON object ↓ Create all Python dictionaries ↓ Create all lists and coordinates ↓ Store everything in memory ↓ Start our analysis This means that even though we only need STREET and BLKLOT , we also load every polygon and coordinate from the dataset. Here's the output that I got: Total parcels: 206,560 Market Street parcels: 808 First five parcel IDs: ['0265003', '0265004', '0265005', '0290012', '0291001'] Time: 4.01 seconds Step 3: Measuring the Memory Usage Instead of simply saying that json.load() consumes a lot of memory, let's measure it. One easy option is memory-profiler . Install it: pip install memory-profiler Now replace the code inside it with this: from memory_profiler import profile import json @profile def process_file(): with open("citylots.json", "r") as f: data = json.load(f) features = data["features"] market_count = 0 for feature in features: if ( feature["properties"] .get("STREET") == "MARKET" ): market_count += 1 process_file() Run: python -m memory_profiler standard_json.py The key line to watch is data = json.load(f) : Line # Mem usage Increment Occurrences Line Contents ============================================================= 5 43.4 MiB 43.4 MiB 1 @profile 6 def process_file(): 7 8 808.9 MiB 0.0 MiB 2 with open("citylots.json", "r") as f: 9 808.9 MiB 765.5 MiB 1 data = json.load(f) 10 11 808.9 MiB 0.0 MiB 1 features = data["features"] 12 13 808.9 MiB 0.0 MiB 1 market_count = 0 14 15 808.9 MiB 0.0 MiB 206561 for feature in features: 16 17 if ( 18 808.9 MiB 0.0 MiB 413120 feature["properties"] 19 808.9 MiB 0.0 MiB 206560 .get("STREET") == "MARKET" 20 ): 21 808.9 MiB 0.0 MiB 808 market_count += 1 22 23 808.9 MiB 0.0 MiB 1 print("Total parcels:", len(features)) 24 808.9 MiB 0.0 MiB 1 print("Market Street parcels:", market_count) You can see a noticeable increase in memory consumption at this point. Why can memory usage be much larger than the original JSON file? Because JSON such as: { "STREET": "MARKET" } becomes several Python objects: dictionary ↓ Python string key ↓ Python string value The same happens for nested geometry arrays and numeric coordinates. The file size on disk is therefore not the same as its memory footprint once parsed. This gives us a baseline to compare against ijson . Step 4: Streaming the JSON File With ijson Now let's solve the same problem without loading the complete document. Install ijson : pip install ijson The key function we will use is: ijson.items() Our dataset has this hierarchy: root │ ├── type │ └── features ├── item ├── item ├── item └── ... Therefore, we can ask ijson to give us each feature individually: import ijson with open("citylots.json", "rb") as f: for feature in ijson.items( f, "features.item" ): print(feature) break The prefix: features.item means: Enter the features array and return each item inside it. Instead of creating one enormous list of parcels, ijson gives us records one at a time. Conceptually: Feature 1 ↓ process ↓ discard Feature 2 ↓ process ↓ discard Feature 3 ↓ process ↓ discard This changes the memory requirements dramatically. Step 5: Performing the Same Analysis With ijson Now let's repeat exactly the same task. Create stream_json.py : import ijson import time start = time.perf_counter() total = 0 market_count = 0 first_five = [] with open("citylots.json", "rb") as f: for feature in ijson.items( f, "features.item" ): total += 1 properties = feature["properties"] if properties.get("STREET") == "MARKET": market_count += 1 if len(first_five) < 5: first_five.append( properties.get("BLKLOT") ) elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start print(f"Total parcels: {total:,}") print(f"Market Street parcels: {market_count:,}") print(f"First five parcel IDs: {first_five}") print(f"Time: {elapsed:.2f} seconds") Output: Total parcels: 206,560 Market Street parcels: 808 First five parcel IDs: ['0265003', '0265004', '0265005', '0290012', '0291001'] Time: 4.58 seconds We no longer have: data = json.load(f) or: features = data["features"] Instead, the program processes each feature directly from the parser: for feature in ijson.items( f, "features.item" ): At any moment, we mainly need memory for: current feature + ijson's parser buffer + small counters + five saved IDs We do not need memory for the complete dataset.

title: Google Open-Sources Harness²: Self-Improving AI Agents Without Retraining
abstract: Google Open-Sources Harness²: Self-Improving AI Agents Without Retraining Google's Harness² lets AI agents improve their prompts, tools, memory, and scripts through two recursive loops without touching model weights. Learn more, including how to run the free demo yourself. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on October 22, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Google Research has open-sourced Harness² (or Harness2 ), a framework that lets AI agents improve themselves without retraining the underlying model. Instead of touching model weights, Harness² rewrites the harness around the model: its prompts, tools, memory, skills, and scripts. Then it carries what it learned into the next task. The code ships under the Apache 2.0 license , alongside a research paper, Harness²: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World , and a project site . The release is already being discussed on X . This article explains how Harness² works and what its benchmark results show, then walks you through Google's free demo and a real benchmark run on Vertex AI. If you're looking for an open-source agent framework for self-improving AI agents, start here. What Is Harness²? A harness is everything around a model that lets it act as an agent: prompts, tools, memory, skills, and orchestration. Harnessing is the work of optimizing it. Today, most teams do it by hand: an engineer watches the agent fail, tweaks the prompt, adds a tool, and tries again. That works for tasks you planned for, but breaks down in what the paper calls an open world , where agents meet tasks nobody anticipated. Harness² automates that tuning "while keeping model weights fixed" (README). There's no fine-tuning and no new training data; only the model's surroundings change. It can edit eight components : Component What it does in the agent System prompt The standing instructions the model reads first Guardrails Rules about what the agent must or must not do Memory Long-term notes carried across steps Skills Reusable instructions for specific kinds of work Tool guidance How and when to use each tool Scripts Helper code the agent can run Subagents Delegated helpers for parts of a task Plugins Middleware that shapes behavior inside the tool loop From the README, the first four build the model's context; tool guidance and scripts define its tool interface, subagents handle delegation, and plugins control middleware. Together they cover nearly everything about how an agent behaves except the model itself. How Harness² Works: Two Levels of Recursion The superscript "2" in the name refers to two loops. One improves the harness for the current task; the other improves how harnesses get improved across tasks. The top loop runs on every task. The highlighted improvement harness persists between tasks and shapes the next round of edits. Loop 1: Task-Level Recursion (Propose—Probe—Compose) Propose : A harness editor suggests invariant (general) and domain (field-specific) edits Probe : The agent reruns the same task with each edited harness Compose : A composer compares the runs and merges the edits that helped The key detail is that Harness² learns "from behavioral contrasts between executions, without ground-truth feedback." It never needs the correct answer, only the difference between two runs of the same task. That matters because in the open world, nobody hands an agent an answer key. Loop 2: Harnessing-Level Recursion After each task, an experience reflector stores the adopted harness and "evidence-supported lessons" in a persistent improvement harness , which guides refinement on the next task. So the first loop makes the agent better at this task, and the second makes the framework better at improving agents on future tasks. You'll see both loops leave files on disk in the demo below. Parallel vs. Sequential Recursion You can spend more compute on Loop 1 with a budget, k , and a mode ( experiment guide ): Parallel proposes k invariant and k domain candidates, then runs k independent compositions over the full pool. It explores wider. Sequential runs k Propose—Probe—Compose steps in a row, carrying the refined harness forward. It refines deeper. The budget drives cost. Each task takes 4k executor rollouts and 3k improver sessions ( run_sweep.py ), so --k 3 means 12 rollouts and 9 improver sessions per task. LAB alone has 1,143 tasks ( experiment guide ), which is why every example here starts with one. Benchmark Results Google tested GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash across four model—harness configurations on three benchmarks. A single step ( k = 1 ) improved both over their base harnesses: Benchmark What it tests Best reported gain WorkBuddy-Bench Office, web, and code tasks Up to +11.5 points LAB Legal work, from Harvey's harvey-labs Up to +11.8 percentage points (partial pass rate) JobBench Professional work tasks Up to +4.5 points These are best-case "up to" figures, not averages, and LAB's is on its Partial score — the fraction of grading criteria passed. The README adds that a larger k "brings further gains," and the paper has per-configuration numbers. These are Google's own results, so independent reproductions will matter. Why This Matters The usual way to make a model better at a job is to train it further, which needs training data, GPUs, and access to its weights. Most teams using a model through an API have none of these. Harness² keeps every improvement in plain files instead: a rewritten prompt, a fixed script, a new guardrail. That has three practical upsides. You can read what changed. An improved harness is text and code, so you can review it and diff it against the original. Harness² even writes down why it adopted each change, as the demo shows. It works with models you can't train. The executor and improver are just model IDs in a config file (setup guide). The release itself pairs GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash as agents with Vertex Gemini or Claude as the improver. It doesn't need an answer key. Refinement comes from contrasts between runs, so it works on tasks nobody has labeled yet. Running the Harness² Demo (No API Key Needed) Google's demo runs both recursion modes with " deterministic editors and real Python executions " and " requires no model credentials ", so it's free. Prerequisites Linux . On Windows, use WSL; on macOS, a Linux VM or container. Python 3.12 . 3.13 is also supported, per pyproject.toml . uv , Astral's Python package manager. git . Step 1: Installing uv curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh curl downloads Astral's installer script. The flags make it follow redirects ( -L ), stay quiet ( -s ) while still showing errors ( -S ), and fail cleanly on a bad response ( -f ). The | sh part pipes the script into your shell, which installs uv into your user directory. Open a new terminal and run uv --version to confirm. pip install uv also works. Step 2: Cloning the Repository git clone https://github.com/google-research/harness2.git cd harness2 git clone downloads the full repository from Google Research's GitHub into a new harness2 folder, and cd moves you into it. Run every later command from this repository root. Step 3: Creating and Activating a Virtual Environment uv venv --python 3.12 .venv source .venv/bin/activate uv venv creates an isolated Python 3.12 environment in .venv , downloading Python if needed. source activates it, so python and installed commands now come from .venv . Your prompt usually shows (.venv) once it's active. Rerun the source line in any new terminal. Step 4: Installing Harness² uv pip install -e '.[render]' -e installs in editable mode, using the source files in place. The [render] extra adds openpyxl and python-pptx for spreadsheet and slide outputs ( pyproject.toml ), and the quotes stop your shell from misreading the brackets. Installing registers the commands used below: harness2 , harness2-demo , harness2-setup , harness2-check , harness2-judge , harness2-report , and harness2-bridge .

title: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident
abstract: Chapter 01 : Alignment assessment summary On August 4, 2026, the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) published a report that detailed some concerning behavior it observed from Claude Mythos 5 during its testing of the model’s cyber capabilities. In AISI’s evaluation, Mythos 5 was given a capture-the-flag (CTF) cybersecurity challenge, in which it was asked to retrieve a protected piece of data (the “flag”) from a simulated network. Internet access was deliberately enabled (this was standard for AISI’s cyber testing at the time, but is no longer). The cyber safeguards we deploy with general release models like Fable 5 were disabled. In nine of AISI’s 43 evaluation runs, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions (i.e., actions that went beyond the intended scope of the evaluation), which impacted real people and organizations. In this post, which is being published alongside an independent report from AISI, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment. Like AISI’s report, we concentrate on the transcript (the complete record of the model’s reasoning and actions) from a single evaluation run. In this run: To capture the flag, Claude Mythos 5 was tasked with breaking into a small network of computers that AISI had built for the test, designed to resemble a real organization’s systems. It attempted—unsuccessfully—a range of approaches that targeted these systems using the methods that the evaluation intended. However, it also quickly found evidence that one of these machines periodically contacted GitHub, which hosts code repositories. After its initial, within-bounds attempts failed, Mythos 5 searched GitHub for a repository that it believed one of the machines downloaded software from automatically. This repository, however, actually belonged to unrelated human developers. Mythos 5 attempted to submit malicious code to the repository, reasoning that doing so would infect the CTF's machine when it next downloaded the code, and, therefore, could compromise the machine. The model then created fake user identities that contacted the maintainer of the repository in an attempt to pressure them into approving the code change. These identifies claimed, falsely, that the code was safe and helpful. The maintainers refused to accept the code change, and Mythos 5’s run eventually timed out. This behavior would have been flagged immediately by our production safeguards on Fable 5, had they been enabled. Nevertheless, this behavior is important to study because the underlying failures here are not necessarily specific to cyber incidents like these. They speak to wider issues with the model’s conduct in evaluation settings; our models’ desired behavior remains a critical part of how we intend to ensure they behave responsibly. Simplified illustration of the pull request initiated by Claude Mythos 5 on a third-party GitHub repository. An outside developer warned about the code containing malware, so Mythos 5 edited the code, used a sock-puppet account to state that the code was now clean, and then uploaded new code with malware. The other eight transcripts were similar to the one described above. In each case, Claude Mythos 5 departed from the intended method for completing a CTF task, and took actions that impacted the real world. From an alignment perspective, we judge the primary transcript (above) to be equally severe or more severe than these other eight. In particular, the primary transcript showed the greatest degree of deception, in the form of Mythos 5’s attempts at social engineering to get its code change approved. Given this (and the degree of the transcripts’ similarities otherwise), we focused on completing one more exhaustive review of the primary transcript, and reviewed the other eight transcripts in less detail. This allowed us to run a large volume of experiments on the primary transcript, and thereby understand the root causes of the issues in more detail. We replayed the transcript from various points, and experimented with altering parts of the model’s prior context to examine how new information would have impacted the model’s behavior. We judge Claude Mythos 5’s misalignment in the primary transcript to be comparable in severity to the Mythos 5 incident we discussed on September 9 , in which the model uploaded a malicious package to PyPi during another CTF task. This assessment is based on our judgment of the model’s behavior in two respects: overreach , or how far the model went beyond the intended scope of the task, and dishonesty , or the extent to which the model misrepresented its actions or intentions. On overreach, the misalignment in this incident was somewhat less severe than in the PyPi incident. Here, before it turned to an attack, Claude Mythos 5 tried several approaches that would have been within the intended scope of the task; a task misconfiguration made it difficult (or potentially impossible) for the model to pursue those within-scope solutions successfully. On dishonesty, however, Mythos 5 went further than in the PyPi incident. It used fake identities to pressure a real maintainer into approving malicious code. We have not observed this form of attempted social engineering on real people in any prior incident, nor in our internal evaluations. We interpret this as a severe form of dishonesty, rather than some new form or category of misalignment: as in the September 9 incident, Mythos 5 used these tactics exclusively in pursuit of its assigned task, and did not pursue any goals of its own devising. On both overreach and dishonesty, we consider the primary incident to be more severe than any of the cases described in our October 9 post . And, for context, this incident is of a very different nature to the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident that was recently investigated by OpenAI and METR. That incident saw several unique misaligned behaviors (like very large-scale coordination between agents to attack a production system), though it did not see a model trying to deceive an individual human in the same way. Newer models appear substantially less likely to initiate the attack described here. We replayed the incident transcript with Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, and a general purpose internal research model that shows capabilities greater than Mythos 5.1. Those three models began the attack between 0% and 13% of the time, relative to 83% for Mythos 5. Our newest models also proved to be much less likely to continue the attack once they realized it was causing real-world harm. Across our testing, in the immediate next few turns of the transcript, Mythos 5 never once decided to stop its attack, and Mythos 5.1 did so only very rarely. But Opus 5.5 and our internal research model stopped spontaneously 10% and 67% of the time—and we expect these rates to understate the true likelihood that these models would have ceased their attacks, since our tests only examined the model’s next few turns. Although we can’t be sure, we suspect that improvements to our alignment training have helped to mitigate Mythos 5’s behaviors in subsequent models. We worked with AISI to complete this analysis of Claude Mythos 5’s alignment. A small number of researchers at both organizations were permitted to analyze the full, unredacted transcripts; a larger group accessed versions with sensitive information redacted. We provided AISI with regular updates on the progress of our assessment, held joint research meetings, and, to assist them in their analysis, shared information not otherwise available to AISI, such as the outputs of our interpretability tooling. We timed our publication to align with AISI’s own report into this incident. Their independent report is available here . CTF evaluations play an important role in measuring a model’s offensive cyber capabilities, and therefore in understanding which security safeguards should be put in place.

title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
abstract: Chapter 01 : Introduction Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa Agrawal Evyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai Zeldovich Nicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit . The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem , however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs . As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development. Introduction Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild. Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules. However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it . Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code . But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V 1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end. We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics . Theorem , our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects , and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code. Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software. The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs— especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work. In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail. Turning tests into proofs To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083 ) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale. To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for. For this project, we started with fuzz tests . In these tests, developers write an entry point 2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try. Fuzzing works by running huge numbers of generated inputs through one entry point to find the inputs that cause a crash. There are infinite inputs, so the search can never be complete. To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB. 3 If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs. We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion).

title: Open call for guest investigators in the life sciences
abstract: Today, we’re inviting members of the life sciences community to apply to work with us on special projects. We’re looking for proposals from principal investigators and their research groups at academic institutions, nonprofits, or government labs who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in causal human biology, structural and computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, and clinical science. You can submit a proposal for a project here . Over 8–12 weeks, guest investigators will work directly with Anthropic researchers on a problem of interest and produce the analyses, artifacts, and tools that will be most helpful for them in their work. Our team will run our models and harnesses at no cost to them. We’ll work together to publish these outputs and open-source the accompanying data and code. Guest investigators retain the rights to their data at every step during their project. They will also have the rights to any independent follow-on research that might come out of our collaboration. We’re looking for applicants who can clearly explain how they would benefit from direct collaboration with Anthropic’s researchers. Applicants should also make a reasonable case that their outputs (e.g., preliminary discoveries, answers to open questions, open-source datasets, or public resources) can be produced within the 8- to 12-week collaboration period. There may be an option for extension beyond the initial collaboration period for some projects. We understand that the results for most open problems of interest will take much longer to validate, but we’re looking for proposals that can produce some preliminary evidence in a relatively short amount of time. We aren’t asking for guest investigators to give us their data, either in the application or during the collaboration, and we’re requesting that applicants include only publicly available information in their application materials. Applications will be open for approximately 14 days, and we’ll strive to notify selected participants by email approximately 14 days after applications close. We look forward to potentially expanding this effort in the future as we learn more about how we can best support the scientific community. This program is one of several initiatives Anthropic is pursuing to invest more heavily in the life sciences and the broader scientific research community. Scientists who would like direct access to our most capable publicly available models for biology can apply to join our Life Sciences Verification Program . We’ve also continued to support researchers through our AI for Science initiative , which provides scientists with Claude credits to accelerate their progress toward making scientific discoveries.

title: Claude Cowork and chat come together for Enterprise
abstract: Chat and Cowork first came together for Pro and Max plans in September. The same unified Claude experience is now generally available for Claude Enterprise plans. Chat and Cowork are now one Claude on web, desktop, and mobile, so your team can ask a quick question or hand over a full project in the same conversation. Agentic work runs in a cloud environment that Anthropic manages, and Claude Enterprise admins control access by role and manage usage with a new Efficient mode. One Claude for every task Team members no longer choose between chat and Cowork before they start work with Claude. Conversations begin as a chat, and a simple question still gets a quick answer. When a task needs to run code or work with files, Claude continues in the cloud and returns the finished document, analysis, or deck. Because the work runs in the cloud, it keeps going after someone closes their laptop, and they can pick it up on the web, desktop, or mobile. Chats, projects, connectors, skills, and plugins carry over to the new unified experience. Organizations are already seeing value from the unified Claude experience across their teams: “Before chat and Cowork capabilities were unified, they were separate experiences that had to be used and managed independently. Bringing them together has made everything simpler, both for our users and administrators. The transition was seamless, nothing broke across our connectors, skills or MCPs, and we’re confident rolling it out more broadly.” Daniel Padilla, CTO of LabX “We no longer have to choose between chat and Cowork. With under ten minutes of prompting, Claude worked through stacks of county, state and federal budgets and public meeting documents, mapped how the funding streams connect, and produced a comprehensive report that would have taken our team weeks. I never had to decide which tool to use for which step. That report will shape our strategic plan and upcoming budget process.” Paul Simpson, CFO and Head of Technology “Bringing chat and Cowork together answers what clients kept asking us, ‘which Claude should I use’ and ‘which one does what’. It adapts to how and where you work across mobile, desktop and browser. Anthropic still encrypts data in transit and at rest and doesn’t use it for model training by default. Claude does agentic work in cloud sessions, each running in its own isolated virtual machine with network egress off by default for Claude Enterprise and connector credentials kept outside the sandbox. Because that work runs in one environment that Anthropic manages, your security team gets central visibility and controls over it. The security best practices guide on the Anthropic Trust Center covers the full architecture. Managing cost Claude Enterprise pricing stays usage-based. Efficient mode is a new setting that keeps the unified Claude experience on Sonnet and Haiku models. Model entitlements set which models each role can use. Spend limits apply at the organization, group, and member level, and pooled group budgets give a group one shared monthly amount to draw from. Getting started The unified Claude experience is generally available today for Claude Enterprise plans. Admins can manage the rollout in Organization settings. Organizations that use zero data retention for Claude Code, a HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys stay on their current configuration.
