title: Claude Duet Safety, Privacy, and Security
abstract: Claude Duet (opens in new tab) is an agent, currently in research preview, that uses a cloud-based computer to do work for you. It can use all the apps and services you've chosen to connect to Claude, and it runs continuously even after you close the app. It can read your inbox, draft replies, book things, and run routines while you are away. Our team runs Claude Duet on our own accounts and we use it for work every day. We built Claude Duet on three principles to guide the agent's behavior: Your information, and what other people share in your connected apps, is handled with discretion, using a new classifier that checks messages Claude Duet drafts before they go out. You stay in control of what it does on your behalf. Claude Duet never sees your passwords, browser cookies, sign-in tokens, or other credentials. Claude Duet is new but the thinking behind it is not. In 2025 we published our framework for safe and trustworthy agents (opens in new tab) , which puts people in control and treats privacy and secure interactions as basic requirements. Since then, we have written about why no single defense is enough (opens in new tab) and why protection inside the model can’t stand alone (opens in new tab) . We also build and operate the infrastructure businesses use to run agents in production through Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab) , and Claude Duet keeps credentials separate from the agent in the same way. It builds on this work, adding the protections that an agent acting for you needs. This post walks through what we added and what we’re still working on. You approve important actions An agent that acts while you’re away has to know when to stop and ask for permission before proceeding, and to do it at the right cadence. Before Claude Duet does something like sending a potentially sensitive message, paying for something, or deleting anything, it shows you the action, the destination, and the content, including every recipient. It then waits for you to approve the action. A separate, automated check runs alongside each action, built on the auto mode classifier from Claude Code (opens in new tab) and extended for Claude Duet. It assesses whether the action matches your intent. The check runs outside the model doing the work so instructions hidden in a page cannot affect the outcome. Some actions stay off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities, banking actions such as moving money between accounts, and accessing someone else's account. Some other steps aren’t covered by a "don't ask me again" rule, however often you have approved them, like paying or sending money, deleting an order, or creating an account. The routines that run while you are away have the same safeguards. We spent a lot of time calibrating how often Claude Duet asks for approval. Approval fatigue is a serious issue, because too many requests teach people to tap through them, sometimes without adequate consideration. We will continue to adjust this calibration over time. For purchases, Claude Duet pays with a one-time card from a wallet like Link from Stripe, limited to that merchant and amount. You see the item and the total, and you approve the purchase in your Link app. Your real card number isn’t shared with Claude Duet or the merchant. Figure 1. Approval flow: the approval card and the separate check sit outside the model, so nothing the agent reads can answer the card. Your information is handled with discretion An agent that reads your email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where different types of information should go. If you ask Claude Duet to send your team a weekly recap, it should include only things everyone on the team already has access to and never private details, like your performance review conversations. To address this, we built a new safety classifier that runs separately from the main model and checks whether each message Claude Duet is about to send contains potentially sensitive information. We categorize this information into two tiers: Never share: We give the most sensitive protection to information like sign-in credentials, full card and bank account numbers, and government ID numbers. Claude Duet is instructed never to share these with anyone, even if you ask. Needs consent to share: Claude Duet will share other private information, such as health or finances, only if you’ve explicitly approved it. Your own request counts as consent, so “send a note to my dentist about my tooth pain” generally won’t need additional approval. Figure 2. Where your information can go: before anything is sent, the check weighs how sensitive the information is and whether you’ve given consent. If Claude Duet is blocked for either reason, it can decide to rewrite the message without the sensitive information and share with you for approval. Claude Duet is still in research preview and these safeguards will occasionally miss something or flag a harmless message. That’s why they work alongside the approval mechanisms above, which are designed to keep you in control of what Claude Duet sends on your behalf. We expect to continue iterating on our classifier as we learn more about how people use Claude Duet. You have visibility into tasks and connected apps You can see what Claude Duet has done and is doing in its task list, where each task has its own page, and steer it mid-task. Claude Duet keeps your conversation history and its memory so it can carry context between tasks, until you delete your history or reset it. Deleting your account wipes everything Claude Duet has stored. The apps you have connected to Claude carry over to Claude Duet, and switching an app off in one place switches it off in both. Disconnecting an app stops new access from that moment, but what Claude Duet already learned from it stays until you reset its memory, which you can do anytime from the app’s settings. Claude Duet also uses the memory from your Claude account, so details Claude remembered from your earlier chats are visible. Credentials and the browser are isolated from the model Claude Duet never sees your passwords, browser cookies, or the sign-in tokens for your connected apps, and it can’t save them to its memory. They only ever pass through separate machines the model can’t access, and the approvals and safety checks that govern what it does run there too. Passwords When a site asks for a password, you type it into a form inside the Claude app. The form encrypts it with a single-use key that exists only on our secure cloud browser machine, for that one single use. It passes the encrypted password unopened to the browser, which types it into the site. The model doesn’t see the password and can’t save or repeat it. Soon you will also be able to sign in with 1Password; Claude Duet will ask for a credential, you will approve that request in 1Password, and the credential will go to the browser without passing through the model. An agent that signs in for you changes phishing in two ways. On one hand, Claude Duet doesn’t hold credentials for you so it can’t be phished for a password, and no hidden instruction can make it reveal a secret it doesn’t have. On the other hand, the sign-in form is itself a target, because anything that asks for a password can be imitated. So Claude Duet’s sign-in form only appears inside the app, during a sign-in you asked for. It never arrives as a link, a text message, an email, or a website other than claude.ai. If something that looks like Claude Duet asks for your password anywhere else, it’s not legitimate. Sign-in tokens When Claude Duet works in a connected app, it follows our Claude Managed Agents design (opens in new tab) so credentials stay out of reach of the agent’s work. Credentials that the agent uses on your behalf, such as a sign-in token for a connected service, never enter the machine where the agent works.

title: The full Claude Platform, available on Google Cloud
abstract: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) is now generally available, giving Google Cloud customers the full set of Claude Platform features, with Google Cloud IAM credentials, billing, and commitment retirement. Claude also remains available via the Google managed offering, where Google is the data processor. Access the complete Claude Platform on Google Cloud With the Anthropic managed offering, Google Cloud customers now receive the full set of Claude API features, with new features and betas shipping the same day they go live on the native Claude Platform. The Anthropic managed offering works with existing Google Cloud IAM credentials, so teams can stay within the tools and permissions they already manage. Billing is through a single Google Cloud invoice and Claude usage draws down your existing Google Cloud commitment. Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) is currently available with US and Global endpoints. “With the Anthropic managed offering, we get the native Claude API with Google Cloud as the access layer. Accessing new features on day one is important. We build AI agents and assistants for Enterprises, and need to bring new Claude capabilities into our product quickly. Using our existing IAM set-up and knowing usage counts towards our Google Cloud commitment made it an easy decision for our team.” Arvind Sundararajan, CTO “Moby, our AI harness for ecommerce brands, runs on Claude. With the Anthropic managed offering, we run Moby on Google Cloud on the same Claude API our team already builds on. Prompt caching is central to how we run Moby cost-effectively at scale, and we’ve kept it while running billing and access through Google Cloud.” Maksim Gorev, Head of AI Engineering What’s included Google Cloud customers using the Anthropic managed offering get the full set of Claude Platform features, so they can: Build and deploy agents with: Claude Managed Agents (beta) (opens in new tab) to power long-running agents, without managing infrastructure Code execution (opens in new tab) to run Python code, create visualizations, and analyze data within an API call Computer use (opens in new tab) to allow Claude to operate a browser or desktop to complete tasks Agent skills (opens in new tab) to teach Claude repeatable workflows so it delivers consistent results Advisor strategy (beta) (opens in new tab) to give agents an intelligence boost by consulting an advisor model Connect to systems and knowledge with: Files API (opens in new tab) for uploading and referencing documents across conversations Citations (opens in new tab) for grounding responses in source documents Web search (opens in new tab) and web fetch (opens in new tab) to augment Claude’s knowledge with current, real-world data from across the web MCP connector (beta) (opens in new tab) to connect Claude to other tools without writing client code Manage cost and performance with: Prompt caching (opens in new tab) for reducing costs and latency on repeated context Batch processing (opens in new tab) for high-volume, asynchronous workloads Fast Mode on Claude Opus 5.5 is also generally available for customers using Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed). Fast mode prioritizes speed, offering up to 2.5x faster output token generation, for rapid iteration, live debugging, and interactive agents where output speed results in a better user experience. Input and output tokens are $8 and $40 per million. See the full list of features available on Claude Models on Google Cloud in our documentation (opens in new tab) . Customers using the Anthropic managed offering also get access to the Claude Console, Anthropic’s development environment for observing and managing agents with Claude. The Console includes tools to write prompts and configure agents, run them on hosted environments, monitor usage and costs, and manage access and security per workspace. Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are available, with new models shipping on the Anthropic managed offering as they launch. Two paths to build with Claude There are two ways to build with Claude on Google Cloud. Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) is built for customers who want day zero access to all beta and generally available Claude Platform features. It’s best for customers who want full Claude Platform feature parity, accessed through Google Cloud. Anthropic operates the service and acts as the data processor. Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed) remains the best choice for customers who need Google Cloud as the data processor, have strict regional data residency requirements, or want native Google Cloud integrations like Model Armor or Agent Engine. Get started The Anthropic managed offering is generally available today. To get started, open Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) (opens in new tab) or explore the documentation (opens in new tab) . If you have an existing discount, please contact your Anthropic or Google Cloud account executive before getting started with the Anthropic managed offering, to ensure your discounts are applied correctly. Discounts cannot be applied retroactively to usage.

title: Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 2
Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1
abstract: Deploying a trained neural network involves more than translating each operator into a GPU kernel. It is a compilation problem with many legitimate answers. For example, when NVIDIA TensorRT builds an engine, it makes interdependent decisions about graph-IR transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. This process is called scheduling. Different scheduling choices can preserve model semantics yet produce very different inference performance, making scheduling central to deep learning compiler optimization. No single scheduling strategy is best for every model and deployment environment. A transformation that accelerates one network may slow another. A kernel that is faster in isolation may interact poorly with fusion, tensor layouts, or memory traffic elsewhere in the graph. Aggressive scheduling may improve performance while violating an application’s accuracy requirement. These coupled, model-dependent effects often appear only after the complete engine is built and measured, making the right strategy increasingly difficult to predict. This post is Part 1 of a two-part series that is intended to develop a clearer way of reasoning about performance optimization. It explores questions such as: What makes one compiled engine better than another? Why can individually promising decisions fail end to end? How should accuracy constrain performance optimization? It introduces the Global Performance Tuner , a feature for automatic performance tuning released in TensorRT 11.1 , and explores these questions through an intuitive example and mathematical framework. What challenge does the Global Performance Tuner feature solve? The following analogy illustrates the motivation for building the Global Performance Tuner feature in TensorRT. Imagine a chef with one excellent dish that has pleased three regular customers for years. One likes spice, another sweet-and-sour flavors, and the third extra salt. The chef combines chili, syrup, lemon, and salt in one standard recipe that satisfies all three. One day, a new fourth customer arrives who dislikes spice. Keeping the chili disappoints the newcomer; removing it risks losing the first customer. The root cause of the chef’s dilemma is the method of adding the seasonings does not scale out: the number of interacting exceptions grows with the customer base, and a change for one customer can degrade the meal for another. Figure 1. One fixed recipe does not scale to conflicting customer preferences A scalable approach keeps the base dish but makes the seasonings configurable. The chef records an appropriate combination for each regular customer. For a new customer with unknown preferences, the chef offers free samples with different combinations, rejects unsuitable variations, and keeps the one the customer likes best. Figure 2. Customize the flavor for each customer Mapping this analogy to deep learning compilation, TensorRT is the chef, its shared pipeline the base recipe, tunable compiler configurations the seasonings, and the compiled engine the finished dish. Each ONNX model is a customer. Performance tuning offers samples, and end-to-end performance reflects customer satisfaction. Historically, TensorRT performance optimization has started with internal KPI models. Engineers study these workloads, identify optimizable patterns, and encode their findings as heuristics in the TensorRT default scheduling strategy. Each heuristic captures expert knowledge and allows users to benefit automatically from optimizations discovered on representative models. As models and deployment environments diversify, this approach leads to a scaling problem similar to the one described in the analogy. A heuristic inspired by one internal KPI model joins the shared strategy and may help familiar patterns while causing a regression for an unseen external model. Adding another check or exception may protect that model, but repeating the process makes the scheduling logic increasingly difficult to extend. The problem appears in three related forms: H euristic sprawl: Each new model-specific heuristic introduces another rule whose interactions with existing rules must be understood and maintained. As these rules accumulate, the code becomes unmaintainable, and improvements for one family of models can unintentionally affect another. Performance-accuracy entanglement: Reduced-precision kernels and other aggressive optimizations can improve performance while introducing numerical differences that exceed an application’s acceptable tolerance. Higher-precision choices may reduce that risk but sacrifice performance. Performance and numerical acceptability therefore cannot always be optimized independently. Performance customization: Scheduling choices that work well for one model or GPU may not work well for another. Encoding every successful choice into one universal scheduling strategy makes it difficult to specialize TensorRT efficiently for a continually expanding range of external models, hardware platforms, and application requirements. Tuning provides a scalable complement to heuristic optimization. Mathematical theory for deep learning compiler performance This section develops an abstract mathematical model of deep learning compiler performance. The purpose is to separate two fundamental questions: What executables a compiler can construct for a model How the compiler selects one from those possibilities for optimal performance Concept: Model, model space Let \(m\) represent a model and \(M\) represent the collection of all models under consideration, called the model space: \(m \in M\) Here, a model is an abstract description of the computation to be compiled. Its concrete representation may be an ONNX graph, a network created through the TensorRT API, a PyTorch model, or another frontend representation that fully specifies the model computation. Concept: Solution, solution space Given a model \(m\) as input, a deep learning compiler constructs an executable output for the target hardware, defined as a solution. The same model can generally be compiled into different solutions under different scheduling policies. Let \(s\) represent one such solution, and let \(S\) represent the collection of possible solutions, called the solution space. s ∈ S = { s 0 , s 1 , s 2 , . . . , s n } s \in S = \{s_0, s_1, s_2, …, s_n\} A solution is an abstraction of executable computation on the target hardware. Concretely, a solution may be a TensorRT engine or a cubin of serialized sequence of GPU kernels. More abstractly, it may also be a compiler’s intermediate representation (IR), provided that the representation uniquely determines the final executable under the remaining compilation process. Each solution also defines a function from the model’s input domain to its output codomain: \(s : X \rightarrow Y\) \(s(x) = y\) Here, \((x,y)\) is an input-output pair for the sequence of GPU kernels that implements the neural network. At this level of abstraction, the model describes the intended computation, while a solution describes one particular way of realizing that computation on the target hardware. Principle of determinism Statement: When both a deterministic program and its complete execution environment remain fixed, the program has a fixed underlying run time. This principle serves as a modeling assumption for performance analysis. Under a rigorous interpretation, the environment includes the input data, target device, software stack, GPU frequency, temperature, power state, system load, and other execution conditions that may influence runtime. In practice, not every environmental variable can be controlled perfectly, so repeated runtime measurements exhibit noise. If this disturbance is modeled as independent Gaussian noise, the average of repeated measurements is the maximum-likelihood estimation of the underlying mean run time.

title: Using AI Agents to Teach Robots Like Microduck to Walk in Simulation
abstract:
Teaching a robot to navigate an obstacle course requires more than a walking policy. It must perceive its surroundings, maintain balance, and adjust its actions when obstacles block the path ahead. Developing these capabilities connects several stages: creating assets and an environment, using physics simulation to model how the robot interacts with its environment, and training and evaluating policies in simulation. NVIDIA RTX Spark serves as a local development hub, supporting AI-assisted planning and policy validation. NVIDIA Isaac Lab provides the robot-learning framework for reinforcement learning in the cloud, while Newton models physical behavior, and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries generate simulated visual observations through RTX rendering. Trained policies return to RTX Spark for local evaluation in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . This post walks through the workflow using Microduck as a reference robot, with Hermes, NVIDIA Nemotron, and Astra assisting with planning and preparation. You’ll learn how to create a simulated obstacle course, train a navigation policy, and evaluate its behavior in simulation—a process you can adapt to your own robots and tasks. This establishes a foundation for physical deployment, where differences between simulation and real-world behavior require further refinement. Figure 1. Workflow overview 1. Create a plan of the obstacle course The workflow begins with a prompt describing the obstacle course and what Microduck must learn. On RTX Spark, Hermes and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt translate that prompt into a step-by-step project plan. The instructions establish the intended task, available resources, expected outputs, and the stages the agents should follow. Use the following example to structure your prompt: Build and test a simulated Microduck obstacle course with navigation and locomotion challenges. Make a photorealistic concept image and have Astra build and test it.
...
Workflow
Use Hermes and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt for preparation and Astra for asset creation and simulation.
...
1. Research and plan
Review official Microduck documentation and summarize capabilities, constraints, and unknowns. Define the course layout, obstacle dimensions, clearances, and intended route.
...
2. Generate the concept
Use a verified Microduck reference image to generate a photorealistic course concept. Check robot appearance, relative scale, and movement space; save prompts and provenance.
...
3. Identify assets
Extract unique reusable assets, group repeated instances, and select representative crops. Record dimensions, locations, and reference limitations; preserve original images.
...
4. Prepare the handoff
Package the plan, robot brief, concept, asset inventory, crops, and execution instructions. Verify required files, delegate to Astra, and wait for confirmed results.
...
5. Create and verify assets
Have Astra enhance references, model geometry in FreeCAD, and apply materials in Blender. Before simulation, verify every asset is completed or demonstrably blocked, with at least one usable model.
...
6. Assemble and test
Verify robot capabilities, assemble the course, and test navigation, challenges, and resets. Provide reproducible instructions and evidence; do not operate physical hardware.
... Local planning includes a brief review of Microduck’s repository and documentation . This review identifies the robot’s capabilities, resources for subsequent work, and details that still need verification. The resulting plan extends beyond asset creation: it outlines environment construction, robot preparation, simulation, training, validation, and deployment. The course needs to test both movement and perception. Microduck must learn to move around obstacles and through constrained spaces while maintaining balance. Use these requirements to guide the proposed layout and the objects needed to construct it. A local image-generation model produces a concept image of the course. Hermes and Nemotron then analyze the image and create an inventory of its visible, reusable assets. Each asset receives an identifier, a description of its visible features, and a cropped reference image. The inventory records where objects are cut off or obscured so that later stages can distinguish visible details from assumptions. Figure 2. Concept image and asset extraction from the obstacle course Hermes combines these outputs into a handoff package: the overall project plan, Microduck research and source links, the concept image, the asset inventory, cropped references, and instructions for the next stages. It then automatically delegates the work to Astra. The package gives Astra the broader project context and asset specifications needed to continue. Figure 3. Turning the task prompt into an environment plan 2. Create simulation assets Using the project plan and references from the previous stage, Astra creates the 3D assets needed for the course. Cropping objects from a larger concept image can result in small, low-resolution references. Before modeling, Astra uses cloud image editing to isolate the objects and produce clearer, higher-resolution images. Astra compares the enhanced references with the original crops, checking that silhouettes, proportions, colors, and distinctive features remain consistent. The enhanced images provide clearer modeling guidance, while the originals document what was visible in the concept image. Dimensions and hidden surfaces that cannot be established from the images are recorded as modeling assumptions. Astra directs FreeCAD to construct the base geometry and editable CAD structure, then uses Blender to add fine geometric details and materials. Both applications run locally through programmatic execution. The generated assets are saved as editable models and exported USD assets, with previews and output checks for review. Figure 4. FreeCAD modeling (left), Blender materials (middle), and the final asset (right), orchestrated by Astra You can also get assets from SimReady Central Library , a free and ungated library of more than 2,000 simulation-ready OpenUSD assets. Reusing them alongside newly generated objects reduces the asset preparation needed to assemble the obstacle course in Isaac Sim. The resulting assets become the building blocks of Microduck’s training environment in simulation. Figure 5. Obstacle-course assets created with Astra and assembled in Isaac Sim 3. Assemble the simulation environment Astra composes the obstacle course using the prepared assets in Isaac Sim. Isaac Sim provides access to Omniverse libraries’ rendering and sensor-simulation capabilities, while Newton models Microduck’s physical behavior, including movement and balance. A robot’s articulated structure and movement are defined in simulation through links, joints, and actuators. These elements establish the relationship between the policy’s actions and the simulated robot. Links represent connected bodies, joints constrain their relative motion, and actuators drive motion. Together, they model a robot interacting with its environment. AI agents can help configure these elements. Simulated sensor observations provide information about the obstacles ahead. As the robot attempts to walk, the simulation captures the consequences of its actions: whether it maintains its posture, makes progress through the course, or stumbles and falls. The result is a complete learning environment: a robot that can act, an obstacle course it can interact with, and a simulated environment that can generate feedback from those interactions. Reinforcement learning (RL) uses this feedback to train robot policies. Figure 6. The assembled environment in Isaac Sim 4. Train the perception and locomotion policy With Microduck and its environment ready, NVIDIA Isaac Lab provides the tools to train and evaluate robot policies at scale. This open-source framework runs many Microduck simulations at once, generating experience that an RL algorithm uses to improve its shared policy.

title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
abstract: Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome. Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder . The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result. This post uses Wordle , a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting. In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models . All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository . The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect. Figure 1: MTRL on SageMaker AI, where the training job invokes the AgentCore-hosted agent once per rollout to sample the policy model, play the game, and report a reward For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word , and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ) adapter on the policy model. Three design points matter for what follows: MTRL is serverless: you pick a base model and the service provisions the training and sampling infrastructure. At the time of writing, it supports the following base models, each trained with a LoRA adapter: We chose GPT-OSS-20B because it has the lowest per-token price of the four and its reasoning effort is controllable per request. See the MTRL documentation for the current list. You don’t choose instances or size a cluster. You pay per million tokens in three dimensions, priced by base model: The 100-step run consumed 491.6 million prefill, 159.7 million sample, and 643.3 million train tokens across 105,486 rollouts in 12 hours 40 minutes. At GPT-OSS-20B list prices in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) at the time of writing, that is about $339: The train dimension dominates and scales with trajectory length, so shorter games and less verbose reasoning cut the bill. The AgentCore runtime bills separately for the vCPU and memory the agent uses. For this run, that was about $79, from the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics at us-east-1 list prices. DescribeJob reports the token counts under BillableTokenUsage . See Amazon SageMaker AI pricing for current rates. To follow this walkthrough, you need the following. See also the MTRL prerequisites . MTRL uses two roles, and one of them has a trust policy that the general SageMaker AI documentation doesn’t mention. Agent runtime role. agentcore deploy creates this role for you. It trusts bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com and needs the AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess managed policy, which lets the agent call the policy model and report rewards. The CDK stack in the sample repository attaches this policy automatically. Training job role. You create this one. It must trust job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com with both sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession , and it needs the AmazonSageMakerJobFullAccess managed policy. Note: The trust principal is job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com , not sagemaker.amazonaws.com . With the generic principal, CreateJob fails with “Could not assume role,” and the message names the correct principal only after retries. Clone the sample repository , set your account and Region in Wordle/agentcore/ aws-targets.json , and deploy: The CLI builds the agent’s dependencies for the runtime’s Linux ARM64 platform, creates the execution role with AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess attached, and deploys through AWS CloudFormation. We recommend it over uploading a code package on the console, where it’s common to get the roughly 700 MB of compiled dependencies or the policy attachment wrong. Note the runtime ARN in the output for the training job. Figure 2: The Wordle agent runtime in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console with status Ready The runtime reads two environment variables from agentcore.json . REASONING_EFFORT=low sets reasoning_effort on every request to the policy model. In our evaluation jobs, low effort used 63 to 83 percent fewer sample tokens per game than medium. REASONING_PROMPT_HINT=true also adds “Reasoning: low” to the system prompt, which is how gpt-oss reads the setting in its Harmony chat format. Neither variable gives the model any hint about the secret word. Figure 3: Runtime environment variables showing REASONING_EFFORT set to low The agent is one file, main.py . Simplified, its entrypoint looks like the following. For your own task, you change the task parsing, the tools, and the reward: Important: The sagemaker_rft_handler decorator does not start an HTTP server by itself. Wrap it with BedrockAgentCoreApp and @app.entrypoint , with the entrypoint decorator outermost. Without this, every invocation times out after 30 seconds. Before spending GPU time, confirm the whole chain works with a payload shaped like the one the training service sends. The repository includes one as Wordle/ payload.json : The fake job ARN is expected to fail, and the way it fails is the proof. Put your own account ID into it first: for a job ARN in another account, the service returns a 403 before it checks whether the job exists, which looks like a broken IAM setup. From the Wordle directory, run: In the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch logs, you see the agent parse the prompt, authenticate to the Job Runtime endpoint, and receive a 400 error reading “Could not find job.” That failure confirms that parsing, authentication, and error reporting work.

title: Orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling with AWS CDK
abstract: Updating the Amazon Sagemaker AI real-time endpoint configuration (changing the instance type, instance count, or environment variables) causes deployments through AWS CloudFormation or the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to fail. SageMaker AI requires you to deregister the scalable target before updating the endpoint, but when you deregister it, CloudFormation can’t track the AWS Application Auto Scaling resources. In this post, we show you how to use a reusable CDK construct with AWS CloudFormation custom resources to orchestrate deregister and register auto scaling automatically during endpoint updates. You can update your endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters in a single deployment without manual intervention. When you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with native CloudFormation auto scaling resources, then change the endpoint configuration and redeploy, several failure modes emerge. The specific failure depends on what you change and how you work around the issue. CloudFormation tries to update the endpoint while the scalable target is still registered. SageMaker AI rejects the update with the following error: SageMaker AI blocks the endpoint update before CloudFormation reaches the auto scaling resources. If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and redeploy with only an endpoint configuration change, the deployment succeeds. However, CloudFormation doesn’t register auto scaling even though it is in the CloudFormation template. Because the auto scaling parameters in the CloudFormation template haven’t changed, CloudFormation doesn’t register the scalable target or re-apply the scaling policy. The endpoint is now running without auto scaling, and there is no error to indicate anything went wrong. If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS CLI and redeploy with auto scaling parameter changes, CloudFormation tries to update the ScalableTarget resource that no longer exists: This failure is notable because the rollback also fails (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED), leaving the stack in a broken state that requires manual intervention in the CloudFormation console to recover. You can use this CDK construct to replace the native AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget and AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalingPolicy CloudFormation resources with three custom resources. These custom resources deregister and register auto scaling around the endpoint update with explicit dependency ordering, enforced by node.add_dependency calls in CDK. The full sequence is: Figure 1: Custom resource orchestration of SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling around a CDK-managed endpoint update. Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy use the CDK provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. Each custom resource has an on_event handler that returns immediately and an is_complete handler. The provider’s waiter re-invokes the is_complete handler on an interval (every 30 seconds) until its readiness check passes. The provider’s total_timeout (1 hour for Register Scalable Target, 15 minutes for Attach Scaling Policy) bounds the wait, so it isn’t limited by the timeout of any single Lambda invocation. A ConfigHash property on each custom resource forces CloudFormation to re-invoke the Lambda functions whenever a configuration value changes. The endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters are defined together because a single ConfigHash drives the auto scaling orchestration. While the construct defines three custom resources, the deployed stack contains more than three Lambda functions. Each custom resource is backed by a CDK cr.Provider , and the provider framework generates its own helper Lambda functions. A synchronous provider (Deregister) adds one framework function. An asynchronous provider (Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy) adds three ( onEvent , isComplete , and onTimeout ) plus an AWS Step Functions state machine that drives the waiter. As a result, the deployed stack contains three custom resources, two Step Functions state machines, and twelve Lambda functions. Five of the resources hold the construct’s own handler code (one for Deregister, and an on_event and is_complete pair for each asynchronous resource), with the remaining seven generated by the provider framework. You don’t write or maintain the framework-generated functions, but they are present in the stack and worth accounting for when you review the deployed resources. In this walkthrough, you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with auto scaling using the provided example stack, then verify that configuration updates work correctly. The walkthrough includes the following steps: The source code is available in the linked GitHub repository . For this walkthrough, you need the following: The endpoint and auto scaling settings are defined together in config/ config.yaml because a single config_hash drives the auto scaling orchestration. A change to either section triggers the full sequence. Edit config/ config.yaml with your values: The endpoint parameters map to the SageMaker AI CreateModel and CreateEndpointConfig APIs. The auto scaling parameters map to the Application Auto Scaling RegisterScalableTarget and PutScalingPolicy APIs. CloudFormation creates the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint, then runs the three custom resources in sequence to register auto scaling. Change a value in config/ config.yaml , for example, update the instance type from ml.m5.large to ml.m5.xlarge , and redeploy: After the deployment completes, verify that auto scaling is still registered and has the updated values: Use the example stack if you’re starting fresh or want a reference implementation. Use the construct directly if you already have a CDK stack with SageMaker AI resources. To integrate with an existing stack, copy the sagemaker_autoscaling/constructs/ directory into your project and add the construct alongside your endpoint resources: This section walks through the key implementation details of SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct . The Deregister custom resource calls deregister_scalable_target before the endpoint update. It handles ObjectNotFoundException for first deployments where no scalable target exists: The dependency is established in CDK: Even though CloudFormation treats the endpoint resource as complete once the update is accepted, the scalable target can only be registered after the endpoint reaches InService . Rather than block a single Lambda invocation on that wait, Register Scalable Target uses the provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. The on_event handler returns immediately, and the provider’s waiter re-invokes the is_complete handler on query_interval until the endpoint is InService . The provider’s total_timeout (1 hour) bounds the wait, not the timeout of any single Lambda invocation: On stack deletion, the on_event handler deregisters the scalable target to clean up. There is a brief window after RegisterScalableTarget returns where the target isn’t yet queryable. Attach Scaling Policy uses the same asynchronous completion pattern: the on_event handler returns immediately, and the is_complete handler reports completion only once the scalable target is queryable, at which point it applies the policy. The provider’s total_timeout (15 minutes) bounds the wait: On stack deletion, the on_event handler deletes the scaling policy to clean up. To avoid incurring future charges, delete the resources: This removes the SageMaker AI endpoint, endpoint configuration, model, Lambda functions, IAM roles, Amazon CloudWatch alarms created by the target tracking scaling policy, and deregisters the scalable target. In this post, we showed you how to use a reusable CDK construct to deregister and register auto scaling automatically to orchestrate SageMaker AI endpoint updates.

title: Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps
abstract: With Amazon Quick Sight layer maps, you can now plot points and routes, like store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport. Geospatial maps help businesses spot patterns that are tied to location, like how a region is performing or where customers are concentrated. Amazon Quick Sight supports this with multiple map types, including point maps, filled maps, and layer maps. When layer maps first launched , you could upload a GeoJSON file to draw custom shape layers, such as sales territories or districts, and join those shapes to a dataset. That handled regions and boundaries well, but it didn’t cover the individual locations inside them or the routes running between them. Layer maps now support two more geometry types from the same GeoJSON workflow: Point and LineString . Points mark specific locations, such as individual store or facility sites. A LineString traces the route between locations, like a delivery path or a flight between airports. Amazon Quick Sight , the business intelligence (BI) capability of Amazon Quick , is a unified BI service. It delivers modern interactive dashboards, natural language querying, pixel-perfect reports, machine learning (ML) insights, and embedded analytics at scale. Amazon Quick brings together AI agents for business insights, research, and automation in one integrated experience, helping you work smarter and faster while maintaining security and access policies. In this post, we walk through the dataset and GeoJSON structure that layer maps require. We also explain how points and lines work in a layer map visual and when to choose each. Finally, we cover advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering geometries, and updating GeoJSON files programmatically. A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a Quick Sight dataset, and a shared key joins the two. How you structure each one determines what the map can show. This section covers what you need before you start and how a GeoJSON file is organized. The following are the prerequisites that you need before creating a layer map in Quick Sight: GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for describing geographic features such as points and lines. The structure of the file is as follows: In Quick Sight, when you configure a layer in a layer map visual, there are two primary settings to consider. The first is the Geometry type to visualize , which sets which geometry from the GeoJSON file renders: Points, Lines, or Polygons. A layer renders one geometry type at a time, so when a file mixes types like the preceding example, only Features of the selected type appear on the map. The second is matching the Shape file key field to the Dataset key field , which links each Feature in the GeoJSON to a row in your Quick Sight dataset. The field names don’t need to be identical, but the values do. The following two examples show this end to end, first a LineString layer and then a Point layer. Consider example data showing a flight from JFK to a destination city like Los Angeles. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows: The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information: Figure 1: Dataset row for the JFK-LAX route, keyed by route_id The route_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per route, and the dataset one row per route. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Lines. Figure 2: The JFK-LAX route drawn as a LineString layer Consider example data showing a retail store location like Long Island City. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows: The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information: Figure 3: Dataset row for a store, keyed by store_id The store_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per store, and the dataset one row per store. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Points. Figure 4: A store plotted as a Point layer Layer map visuals now support LineString geometry, connecting an ordered list of coordinates into a single path. As covered in the data structure section, each route is one feature, and its coordinates are the ordered positions the map connects in sequence. Use lines when the relationship between locations is what you want to show, such as flight paths, delivery routes, shipping lanes, or pipeline segments. The visual draws each path from the coordinates in your GeoJSON file rather than generating it from your data at load time. A field from your joined dataset can determine the line color encoding, so you can group routes by whatever that field represents. In addition to color, you can customize lines with width and opacity controls to adjust visual prominence and clarity on the map. The join key in the GeoJSON properties object ties each LineString to the dataset row behind its tooltip and color. For example, an airport operations team might map the flights leaving New York (JFK) on a given day. The GeoJSON file holds one LineString per route, keyed by a route ID that joins to the dataset. Each line starts at JFK and ends at its destination, such as Los Angeles, Chicago, or Miami. The dataset supplies the origin, destination, and carrier that show up in the tooltip. Figure 5: Flights leaving JFK drawn as LineString routes to multiple destinations Amazon Quick Sight offers a native point map visual type that geocodes location names automatically and refreshes with your SPICE schedule or Direct Query connection. It supports dynamic point sizing, color encoding, and point styles such as cluster points and heatmap density gradients. It works best with data that changes frequently and where you want the map to respond to those changes visually. With the added support for GeoJSON point layers in layer map visuals, Quick Sight now offers a second point mapping capability with a few key differences. Layer map visual points use a uniform marker size and don’t support geocoding, so you provide explicit coordinates in the GeoJSON file. In return, you can control the viewport precisely, locking the map to an exact geographic region, and disabling panning and zooming. The following table summarizes the key differences: Choose layer map visual points when: Consider a retail brand whose regional managers use a Quick Sight dashboard to track store performance across a metro area. The GeoJSON file contains a Point feature for each store with a store ID property that joins to the dataset. The dataset holds the metrics (store type, monthly revenue, daily foot traffic) that drive the tooltip and color encoding. You position the map at the zoom level covering the metro area, then disable map navigation so the map renders at a consistent view on every load. Managers can’t accidentally zoom out to a national or global view. Figure 6: Store locations as points with map navigation disabled to lock the metro-area view The previous sections cover a standard layer map setup. Use the following techniques when you need more control over what readers see, want to combine geometry types in a single view, or need geometry that changes over time. When you need to control the viewport in layer map visuals, you can pan and zoom to the view you want manually. Then disable map navigation to lock it in place. For use cases where you need more precise boundaries or programmatic control, you can set the exact viewport coordinates through the visual definition using the Quick Sight APIs. The layer map visual stores its viewport configuration in the MapState property within ChartConfiguration . This property accepts two fields: Although the bounds property is not exposed on the console, you can set these bounds when working with the dashboard definition JSON for programmatic asset management.

title: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations
abstract: Plant breeding decisions depend on data that spans genomics, field trials, imagery, environmental conditions, and model outputs. Bayer Crop Science runs hundreds of machine learning (ML) model configurations against this data across crops, regions, and teams, and each run needs to be repeatable and governed. To meet that requirement, Bayer built the Connected Decision Engine (CDE), a system for deploying, orchestrating, monitoring, and reusing ML workflows. CDE gives breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and data engineers a consistent way to run analytics while preserving execution history and operational controls. As adoption grew, the bottleneck moved from running workflows to understanding them. Explaining a result meant piecing together context from APIs, documentation, metadata stores, dashboards, and logs. A user who wanted to know why a workflow failed, what a model did, or where a result came from still had to know which system to inspect. To close that gap, Bayer built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent, natural language interface over CDE. A supervisor agent routes each question to a specialist agent, the specialist retrieves context from the relevant system, and the user receives an answer without navigating the operational stack. In its first phase, ADE resolves about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop. ADE runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , an AWS service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore let the team focus on agent behavior instead of building and operating its own agent hosting, session isolation, and tool access layer. Three AgentCore capabilities drove that choice: a managed runtime that isolates each user session, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped tool access through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, that keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code, and a framework-agnostic design that let the team bring its own LangGraph orchestration and choice of models. To prepare for launch and to operate ADE afterward, Bayer engaged AWS Unified Operations . The engagement provided a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and a generative AI Domain Specialist Engineer (DSE), who worked as an extension of the ADE team from design through production. The TAM, as Bayer’s strategic advisor, brought an established understanding of Bayer’s operating model and business priorities. The DSE brought generative AI domain expertise on AWS. In three technical standups each week, the team reviewed and made design decisions. The DSE built working knowledge of the ADE workload and how the Bayer team operates, so technical guidance reflected both AWS service behavior and Bayer’s context. This post follows that journey: the ADE architecture, five design decisions made during the build, the work to prepare the platform for production, and how it is operated after launch. ADE is organized into four layers: the user experience, agent orchestration, specialist agents, and the tools and data sources those agents call (Figure 1). Users reach ADE through a React web front end, and requests pass through an identity proxy for Microsoft Entra ID before they reach the agents. GitHub Actions builds the agent container images, pushes them to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) , and deploys them to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the agents, and because the runtime is framework-agnostic, the team runs its own LangGraph-based orchestration on it directly. The team chose LangGraph for its explicit graph-based control flow and checkpointing for multi-step workflows. LangGraph orchestrates the workflow, with a Supervisor Agent as the entry point that classifies each request, selects a specialist, and combines results when a question spans domains. The data plane is separated by responsibility. Amazon DynamoDB stores LangGraph checkpoint state. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL stores session records, user feedback, and analytics. Amazon ElastiCache caches agent responses with a time to live (TTL). Domain content in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is embedded with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and indexed in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Amazon CloudWatch captures runtime and application telemetry. AgentCore Gateway exposes backend APIs to agents as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code. Figure 1: Agentic Decision Engine architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore ADE runs 22 specialist agents in production, each scoped to one domain with its own tools and data sources. For example, the Domain Expert Agent answers conceptual questions through RAG. The Operational Agent retrieves live workflow status and results from CDE. The Troubleshooting Agent analyzes operational telemetry. The Visualization Agent generates charts or returns existing dashboards. A customer-specific Models as Skill pattern converts model code and documentation into skill definitions stored in a central registry, so agents answer model-specific questions from the model’s implementation instead of generic model knowledge. When a breeder asks, “Why did my phenotyping workflow fail yesterday?”, the supervisor classifies the intent and routes the request to the Troubleshooting Agent. That agent reads the workflow’s telemetry in CloudWatch and its status from the CDE API through AgentCore Gateway, identifies the failure point, and returns a diagnosis through the supervisor (Figure 2). The breeder doesn’t search logs directly. With the Troubleshooting Agent, a diagnosis that once took over an hour of manual log-hunting and waiting for engineer support now takes under 10 minutes. Figure 2: ADE request flow: intent classification, cache lookup, specialist routing, and response The Unified Operations TAM and DSE took part in the following decisions as members of the working team, not as an escalation point after the fact. That let Bayer test each design against AWS service behavior before committing to it, while keeping ownership of the architecture and the final call. AgentCore runtime provides isolated sessions that preserve execution context across invocations within a session’s lifecycle. That context isn’t a durable store for a multi-step workflow. ADE writes LangGraph checkpoints to DynamoDB so the graph can resume after scale-out events, restarts, or session boundaries without depending on one execution environment remaining available. Principle: Use the runtime session for active execution, and persist the state required to resume or reconstruct the workflow in a durable service. Bayer standardizes on Microsoft Entra ID for user identity, while ADE’s services authorize each other with AWS-native mechanisms. Rather than force one token across every trust boundary, the team gave each boundary its own mechanism. Entra ID remains the source of user identity. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) authorizes service-to-service calls. AgentCore Gateway outbound authorization handles access to downstream CDE services. A request interceptor AWS Lambda function performs custom validation and passes the authorization attributes that downstream tools require. The team worked through the token contract at each hop with the DSE. Principle: Identity failures in agent systems cluster at the transitions between user identity, agent identity, and tool identity. Define the issuer, audience, claims, scopes, and credential lifetime at every hop instead of reusing a token that is valid for one boundary at the next. During the build, the team evaluated a newer model version with reasoning mode enabled. For that version, the combination of tool use and structured output that ADE depends on was not compatible with how its agents were implemented.

title: 百度世界2026前瞻：10+重磅分論壇，全面解碼AI時代的智慧組織進化路徑
abstract: 百度世界2026前瞻：10+重磅分論壇，全面解碼AI時代的智慧組織進化路徑 量子位的朋友們 2026-10-23 15:35:51 來源： 量子位 10月21日，百度官方公眾號發文披露了百度世界2026分論壇的更多議程資訊。 企業AI轉型正在走向深水區，從單點工具和業務場景提效，向系統性的組織重構延伸。麥肯錫曾在《組織狀態報告2026》中指出，儘管AI被視為新一輪生產力革命的重要驅動力，但真正將其轉化為經營業績的企業仍是少數，背後的關鍵在於，不少企業仍將AI轉型停留在“工具升級”層面，卻忽視了更本質的“組織重構”。如何將AI能力融入組織，轉化為持續的生產力，將成為影響企業未來競爭力的關鍵。11月12日，百度將在百度世界2026大會上聚焦“智慧組織”議題，或將提出AI時代的組織進化範式。 10月21日，百度官方公眾號發文披露了百度世界2026分論壇的更多議程資訊。本屆大會設定10+場分論壇，圍繞“AI驅動組織躍遷”、“AI辦公與知識工作”、“技術、行業與生態”三大方向展開，涵蓋組織進化、智慧體規模化落地、AI辦公、AI+自進化、垂直產業增長、超級個體能力進階等議題，為企業和開發者推進智慧組織建設提供多維度的實踐參考。 看點一：覆蓋AI組織重構全鏈條，揭秘“智慧組織”進化方法論 AI時代，組織形態或將朝著以人和智慧體編隊協同的方向演進，這一轉變涉及人機協同機制、工作流重構、組織文化變革與安全治理等多個環節。本屆大會分論壇議題將覆蓋組織自上而下進行AI重構的全鏈條，解碼企業如何將AI內化為組織能力，構築競爭優勢。 「組織進化：AI驅動組織躍遷」分論壇上，百度將分享內部智慧組織建設的實踐與最新成果，進一步呈現“內化AI能力”如何落實到企業執行之中。據悉，該論壇將圍繞崗位邊界重構、“組織looping”飛輪、AI資產沉澱及智慧體安全、開啟人才上限等議題，剖析組織如何在持續迭代中實現自我進化，激發組織活力。 「Agent紮根研發生產：如何從“用AI”到“成為AI企業”」分論壇將圍繞智慧體底座、資料與知識、場景選擇、組織與人才四個方面，梳理企業從單點應用AI走向體系化轉型的關鍵條件，分享AI原生企業構建案例。 看點二：從超級個體到超級組織，解碼AI從個人提效走向組織增智 隨著智慧體、數字人等AI應用加速融入企業生產經營場景，AI的價值釋放逐漸從個人提效轉向依託團隊協作、組織增效。本屆大會分論壇還將展示百度在智慧體領域的最新佈局，分享智慧體、數字人等在高價值知識工作場景中的產品與案例，為企業和開發者從具體場景入手、推動個人提效向組織增智延伸提供實踐思路。 「搭子進行時·北京站 — 智慧體如何從辦公桌走向生產線」分論壇將圍繞通用智慧體演進趨勢、企業級應用、生態共建等議題，結合百度搭子融入個人辦公、團隊協作和企業業務的實踐，分享以智慧體賦能超級個體、提升組織生產力的方法論，進一步推動產業智慧。 「超級智慧 全球上崗 — 成就超級個體 打造超級組織」分論壇將從使用者、團隊協作與全球化應用三個視角，聚焦超級個人與超級組織的進化路徑、企業Agent對組織協作的重構，以及AI辦公全球化發展新機遇等議題，討論AI如何從個人效率工具走向組織級生產力。 數字人分論壇將聚焦數字人Agent的全新升級，探討數字人Agent在品牌營銷、跨境出海、售後服務、企業內訓等多個業務場景應用，呈現數字人如何從虛擬形象升級為智慧組織中可被排程、可複用、持續創造價值的生產力。 看點三：從組織實踐到行業方案，展現智慧組織在千行百業的落地路徑 智慧組織的落地，還需要與不同行業的業務需求和場景特點緊密結合。本屆大會分論壇中，百度還將聯合合作夥伴，圍繞具身智慧、品牌營銷、遊戲等領域，交流AI融入業務流程與組織協作的實踐經驗，為形成可供行業借鑑的解決方案提供思路，助力千行百業向智慧組織演進。 「具身智慧如何從場景驗證走向商業落地」分論壇將圍繞世界模型、多模態具身認知、物理推理、具身大腦、行為理解及模擬互動等議題，探討提升具身智慧對真實環境的理解與任務執行能力的技術路徑，推動其從場景驗證走向可迭代、可規模化的產業應用。 「如何用AI實現營銷全週期閉環：洞察·創意·最佳化」分論壇將聚焦內容生產、組織協作與科學投放三大環節，聚焦數字人讓廣告內容生產提效10倍、AI數字員工推動營銷經驗在組織內複用、科學演算法將以往“憑經驗拍板”的預算分配轉化為確定性增長等實踐，呈現AI融入營銷全鏈路的解決方案。 「從提效到AI原生，如何找到遊戲產業增長新曲線」分論壇將聯合國內前沿AI遊戲團隊，圍繞遊戲開發、AI NPC及智慧安全等議題，探討大模型和Agent重塑遊戲開發流程，融入角色互動與玩法設計的實踐，推動AI從輔助遊戲開發走向AI原生遊戲創造，拓展“千人千面”的遊戲體驗。 看點四：探討AI前沿技術趨勢，助力科學發現程序 AI技術的進化速度，深刻影響著產業落地的廣度與深度。當前，智慧體等技術正加速向自我進化方向演進，RSI成為行業熱議話題。本屆大會還將聚焦RSI、AI4S等前沿議題，探討AI技術變革趨勢及其在產業場景中的應用前景。 「RSI如何重塑科學工程研發」分論壇將分享智慧體自我進化的前沿趨勢，聚焦RSI在材料研發、晶片設計、量子計算與可控核聚變等領域的應用探索，討論自我改進系統在解決複雜科學與工程問題中的應用價值與能力邊界。 「AI4S如何加速科學研究與生命健康創新躍遷」分論壇將聚焦AI for Science與AI for Healthcare，解析算力、雲、大模型及智慧體等技術在科學研究與生命健康領域的應用，呈現AI在助力科研方法創新、生命科學複雜問題求解及新藥全流程研發中的作用。 據悉，除10+場分論壇外，本屆大會還設定1場主論壇、30餘場AI公開課及6000平米AI展區。百度創始人李彥宏將在大會開幕式上發表主題演講，分享對智慧組織演進趨勢的思考。此外，百度還將釋出“芯雲模體”全棧AI最新進展，為企業和開發者推進智慧組織建設提供技術與產品支援。 title: 又一國產決策模型釋出！準確率超過微軟和Jev等決策模型
abstract: 又一國產決策模型釋出！準確率超過微軟和Jev等決策模型 量子位的朋友們 2026-10-22 17:07:05 來源： 量子位 10月22日，螞蟻數科正式釋出決策模型 LingDT-Decision-1.0。 10月22日，螞蟻數科正式釋出決策模型 LingDT-Decision-1.0。該模型專為快速決策打造，在處理結構化決策任務時，具備準確率更高、響應更快、Token成本更低等優勢，尤其適合產業AI場景。LingDT-Decision-1.0提供4B和27B兩個版本，目前，模型已經在螞蟻數科 DTMaaS 平臺上線，開發者可限時免費體驗。 螞蟻數科團隊在客服、風控、金融等真實業務場景測試顯示，在處理同樣任務時，LingDT-Decision-1.0相比於大語言模型，可將Token消耗降低超90%，響應時效提升10倍，並且效能表現更優。 相比於其他決策模型，LingDT-Decision-1.0首創支援原生多選與按序決策能力，更適配企業真實應用場景。在23項開源評測基準中，LingDT-Decision-1.0的綜合評分超過了Microsoft-Decision-1、Jev 1.13.等熱門決策模型，LingDT-Decision-1.0的27B版本在同參數模型中取得最高準確率。 （圖注：LingDT Decision 的4B/27B 版本的優勢區域，覆蓋了相關尺寸包括Jev、MS Decision、GLiDE等決策模型，表現出極強的綜合性價比） 專為決策任務設計，Token消耗直降超90%，更快更準 在企業實際應用中，存在大量高頻的決策類任務。 例如，在客服場景中，當收到“這個訂單已經三天了還沒發貨，請儘快處理。”的問詢後，AI需要快速進行一系列判斷和決策：問題型別（退款、催單還是投訴？）、工單緊急度（是否需要優先處理）、歸屬部門（工單派到哪個部門）以及風險判斷（是否需要人工接管）。 傳統大語言模型在這類場景中存在明顯短板。大語言模型通常需要逐字（Token）進行推理，再生成輸出文本，鏈路長、成本高，也更容易出現錯誤，效能不夠穩定。 決策模型正是針對這些痛點而設計，它的目標不是生成文本，而是做出快速、準確的判斷。因此，天然適合承擔企業業務中的高頻決策型任務，如意圖判斷、工具選擇、規則分類和結果打分等。 目前，LingDT-Decision-1.0 模型目前已在螞蟻數科的智慧客服、安全風控、金融應用等真實業務場景展開測試。它的核心思路，是把大模型從“先生成結構化答案，再做後續解析”，轉變為“在限定選項中直接做判斷”。這樣不僅減少了因輸出不穩定帶來的格式問題，也讓原本繁瑣的解析和校驗流程變得更加簡單。 例如，在資料標註場景中，相比 DS-V4-flash，Token消耗降低約97%，處理時效提升約10倍；在智慧客服場景中，相比 Qwen-3.7-flash，Token消耗降低90%，處理時效提升約1倍，同時風險識別準確率由76%提升至89%。 在金融應用場景中，在意圖識別、工具呼叫、幻覺檢測等任務中，處理時效提升約5倍，工具組合完全匹配率達提升約 2.6 倍，同時幻覺召回率由 44% 提升至70%，風險發現更敏感。 綜合來看，LingDT-Decision-1.0在多個真實場景中穩定體現出成本更低、響應更快、判斷更準的優勢。與此同時，它還能以一套模型適配多類判定任務，接入更簡單、維護更省力，因此也更容易在不同業務場景中複用和推廣。 打造下一代決策式模型，兩大功能全球首發 相比其他決策模型，螞蟻數科 LingDT-Decision-1.0 更加強調面向企業真實應用場景打造。除了判斷、單選、分類、評級等基礎能力外，LingDT-Decision-1.0 還首創推出原生多選與 按序決策（DAG）功能，能夠更好適配企業業務中複雜、多步驟的決策需求。 在企業場景中，更普遍的並不是“選一個”，是“識別一組要處理的事項，並按順序執行”。例如當用戶提出：“我要退款、關閉續費、補開發票，但不要登出賬號。”單選往往只能識別“退款”這一主訴求，容易漏掉其他需求。而多選能一次識別所有訴求；按序決策還能進一步判斷：退款需先核驗，關閉續費可先執行，發票處理可能要等退款結果。因此，多選和按序決策更貼近真實業務流程，也更能提升準確率和最終處理效果。 在原生多選能力上，LingDT-Decision-1.0允許一項任務同時命中多個候選，適配多標籤識別、複合意圖和工具組合等需求；在按序決策能力上，模型能夠按照任務之間的依賴關係完成多步決策，更貼近金融、風控、客服等真實業務流程。 覆蓋23項主流開源評測基準的測試結果顯示，LingDT-Decision-1.0的27B版本綜合評分（90%x單選評分+10%x多選評分）位居第一，準確率超過Microsoft-Decision-1、Jev 1.13.0、Fastino/GLiDE等熱門決策模型。其中，在多選任務上，LingDT-Decision-1.0的4B和27B版本的準確率表現超過Microsoft-Decision-1、Jev 1.13.0、Star-lux等16個決策模型，體現出原生多選能力在多標籤與組合判定任務中的優勢。在單選任務上，位居第一梯隊。 （圖注：通過單選/多選能力的2維圖展開 體現了LingDT Decision 4B/27B 在單選&判斷能力 屬於Tier-1 超越絕大多數同尺寸模型；而“原生多選能力”斷檔式領先） 本文由螞蟻提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 螞蟻 量子位的朋友們 科大訊飛首發星辰TaaS平臺，讓Token真正成為千行百業的生產力 2026-10-23
