title: Better speech synthesis for audiobooks
abstract: Text-to-speech systems — which convert written text into synthetic speech — display impressive naturalness in applications such as chatbots and virtual assistants, where interactions last seconds. But they tend not to fare as well with longer-form content. When applied to audiobooks, for instance, conventional text-to-speech (TTS) models fail to reliably change speaking style between characters, as a human narrator would. This creates two problems for listeners: (1) distinguishing narration from dialogue and (2) identifying which character speaks which lines. To address this problem, the Audible technology team is using controllable TTS, meaning the ability to control dialogue delivery with natural-language speech descriptions (e.g., "speak in an enthusiastic, high-pitched voice"). This allows the TTS model to leverage the deep textual understanding of large language models (LLMs) to synthesize high-quality speech. Our approach involves three key innovations. First, we developed a novel data synthesis pipeline to produce speech data captioned with high-quality descriptions of speech characteristics. Training on this data enables our model to understand captions and produce audio consistent with them at inference time. Second, we created a system that automatically profiles characters in books and identifies their dialogue with 97% accuracy. It also provides captions for that dialogue, which act as stage directions for the model. Third, we used the first two techniques to synthesize audiobooks featuring distinct character voices, improving dialogue differentiation by 3.7 points on a MUSHRA (multiple stimuli with hidden reference and anchor) test, a standardized method where listeners rate audio quality on a scale from 0 to 100. Across tests in both English and Spanish, we observe statistically significant improvement in listening experience for eight out of ten voices. TTS for audiobooks Subtle defects in synthetic speech, such as unnatural prosody or monotone delivery, are tolerable for short stretches but become increasingly grating over time — and audiobook listeners engage with the same voice for 10 to 15 hours per book. This is why off-the-shelf TTS models often fail to produce enjoyable, natural audiobook narrations. Furthermore, general-purpose TTS models are designed to process individual utterances with minimal context. That’s a reasonable approach when responding to questions like "What's the weather today?", but it’s inadequate for audiobooks, where narrative coherence depends on understanding the surrounding story context. A TTS model reading dialogue needs to know whether the speaker is the protagonist confronting an antagonist or a minor character making small talk, information that may only be available in earlier chapters. Finally, general-purpose models struggle to produce character voices in a consistent and natural way across the span of an entire book, often voicing a character in a markedly different way in chapter 1 than in chapter 10. Controllable text-to-speech I. The data synthesis pipeline Whereas conventional TTS models are trained on text-speech pairs, a controllable-TTS model also requires annotations that describe how the speech sounds. The speech in the training set also needs to be highly expressive, covering the wide variety of dimensions — pitch, speaking rate, character voices, emotions, speaking styles, etc. — the model must control. Previous TTS models couldn't handle that kind of expressivity, so most existing training data is neutral in tone. We expanded the training sets through two approaches: new recordings and human captioning of existing audio data. While there are some datasets that include descriptions of prosodic features, each has its own description format: some are long, some are short, and some use single tags. This limits the flexibility of model inputs and tends to make the model overfit the formats of specific datasets. To improve generalization, we use LLMs to rewrite the original prompts into different formats, varying length, verbosity, and structure (single tags vs. free-form natural language). Second, the human-in-the-loop data collection procedures do not scale to the size of the datasets we need. Therefore, we complement the collected data with a large amount of synthetic data. We use two approaches: 1. Expert-model pipeline. This approach uses expert models and signal-processing algorithms such as pitch extraction, speaking rate extraction, and emotion detection to extract numerical features from audio data. We then feed these features and classification labels into an LLM to generate speech captions. 2. Speech captioner. We developed a model that performs a task opposite that of controllable TTS: it takes speech and outputs a description of prosodic features. Using this speech captioner, we can annotate larger amounts of data. We use the annotated data as seed data to train the initial controllable-TTS model, and we also use it to continue training the speech captioner itself. We then use these models to generate synthetic data, and we improve them both iteratively to create a synthetic-data flywheel. II. BookLLM: Adapting to the audiobook domain The audiobook domain presents additional challenges for a controllable-TTS system, since different characters need to have distinct but consistent voices. For this, we developed BookLLM, a separate component that leverages off-the-shelf LLMs to identify unique characters and uses information in the book — for instance, age, gender, personality, and role — to define their voice characteristics. Then the model determines which character speaks where and captions dialogue with descriptions of how it should be spoken. We evaluated BookLLM on 25 English and Spanish books in the mystery, sci fi, and romance genres. We collected ground truth annotations using two human annotators. In English and Spanish, the system achieved 97% and 94% accuracy, respectively, in identifying which character speaks where, including distinguishing between narration and dialogue III. Bringing it all together Bringing the two components together yields a complete audiobook-synthesis pipeline. Given a new book, BookLLM first reads the entire text to build a cast list: it determines the unique characters, ranks them by importance, and derives a voice description for each. Rather than inventing an unbounded set of voices, it assigns each character a distinct profile from a curated voice catalogue, deliberately maximizing the contrast between the most prominent characters so that listeners can tell them apart. Minor and one-off characters fall back to the default narrator, avoiding a proliferation of barely used voices. BookLLM then walks through the book and attributes every passage to a speaker — the narrator or a specific character — and, for each line of dialogue, writes a caption describing how it should be delivered, such as "whispering nervously" or "shouting in anger". These captions are exactly the kind of natural-language speech description that the controllable-TTS model was trained to follow. At synthesis time, each unit of text is passed to the TTS model, together with its speaker's voice profile and, if necessary, its stage direction caption. Because a character's voice profile is fixed once at the book level, the model renders that character consistently from beginning to end, avoiding general-purpose models’ tendency to drift, or voice a character differently in chapter one than in chapter ten. The per-line captions layer moment-to-moment expressivity on top. The result is a full-length audiobook in which characters sound distinct, consistent, and expressive that ultimately provides a more delightful listening experience.

title: Built for Agents: The Case for Spark Declarative Pipelines
abstract: AI agents now write a growing share of production data pipelines ( over 70% of SDP pipelines on Databricks are now created by agents) which raises the stakes in two areas: (1) every attempt an agent makes costs compute and time, so iterations need to be cheap and efficient to run; and (2) code review become a critical gate, so the code needs to be succinct, readable, and correct. Apache Spark® offers two programming models to author your pipelines, procedural and declarative, and they differ in what you write, in what Spark can check before it runs, and in how much a mistake costs. We benchmarked both with the same agent on the same jobs, and declarative came out safer, cheaper, and leaner. A procedural pipeline is code that tells Spark how to build each dataset, step by step. The only way to know whether it works is to run it. A declarative pipeline describes the datasets you want and leaves Spark to decide how to build them. This is akin to when you prompt an LLM, and it figures out how to do it (by using the right skills & tools). This is best illustrated in code to see how a simple typo will fail: Bugs come in two flavors. Structural ones you can catch by reading the pipeline: an unresolved column reference, a table that doesn’t exist yet, a config change that is not allowed. Silent ones only show up in the output when the run finishes and the answer is wrong. A declarative pipeline can be checked for structural bugs before it runs, similar to how data flow in a typed language like Rust can be checked at compile time. Because a declarative pipeline is a description rather than a run, Spark can answer three kinds of questions by reading it: In procedural PySpark, the AI coding agent writes the data operations, such as filtering invalid rows and joining tables. It also writes code to run the pipeline’s steps in the right order and save their results. This supporting code repeats much of the same boilerplate across pipelines. In declarative pipelines, the AI agent defines each dataset and the query that produces it. Spark handles the execution order and saves the results. With Spark handling that boilerplate, the agent writes less code, and the team has less to review and maintain. We tested 22 data engineering tasks. Each task looked like a real ticket: it described a problem and specified the table, column names, and data types that the pipeline had to produce. The agent could choose any implementation as long as the output matched those requirements. For each task, we generated 12 different input datasets with the kinds of messy values found in production data. The agent wrote a new pipeline for every dataset using procedural PySpark and another using Spark Declarative Pipelines. That produced 264 builds per approach and 528 in total: 22 tasks × 12 datasets × 2 approaches. All builds used Opus 4.8. We ran each pipeline and checked its output against the required table. The automated grader did not know which approach had produced the result. Declarative pipelines first went through Spark's dry run. If a build failed, the agent could revise it and try again, up to a fixed limit. You can rerun the whole thing yourself from the public repository : the setup, prompts, datasets, grader, and the results behind every number. Both ways finished nearly every task, with 255 of 264 completed procedurally and 258 of 264 completed declaratively, so either one gets you to a working pipeline. What differs is everything around that: when mistakes surfaced, how much code it took to fix, and how consistent the output was. We cover the three advantages of declarative pipelines below, followed by two caveats. 1. Validating before the run made declarative pipelines ~34x less time A pipeline's mistakes surface before execution, during a run, or not at all. Procedural pipelines stopped none before execution because they have no pre-execution stage. To find a structural error, Spark had to run the pipeline on a cluster until it reached the broken step. Across the builds we measured, procedural runs used 596 executor-seconds, compared with 17 for declarative runs. Dry-run validation of declarative code caught structural errors early and reduced compute by 34X. 2. Declarative pipeline code was half the size of procedural pipelines Among the completed builds, declarative pipelines were about half the size, with a median of 64 lines compared with 131 for procedural pipelines. The procedural implementations also varied more. For the same job, some used Spark transformations while others loaded the data into memory and processed it one row at a time. Both passed on the test data, but the in-memory version can fail when the data grows. Across the benchmark, 19 procedural builds used this shortcut. None of the declarative builds did. Shorter, more consistent code gives a team less to review and one pattern to maintain. 3. On logic errors, the two came out level Those are the two advantages. When running the tests, we also identified two caveats. First, a dry run can only catch structural mistakes. It cannot catch a silent one: a pipeline that runs cleanly and returns the wrong answer, which is the more dangerous kind. On that count, the two came out even: their silent-error rates were within roughly 15% of each other, a gap too small to be a real difference. Declarative makes structural mistakes cheap to catch; it does nothing for logic, which still needs tests and review. 4. Declarative spends more up front to save more later Declarative spends more in one place. The agent iterates on the dry run, retrying until the pipeline is sound, so it does more of its thinking in tokens up front rather than discovering problems on a cluster later. The tokens are a fixed, one-time spend, paid while the pipeline is being written; the amount does not change based on your data size or how often the pipeline runs. Wasted cluster compute is the opposite: it recurs on every bad run and grows with the data, so the more you process, the more a bad build costs. Paying a fixed cost up front to avoid one that keeps growing only looks better as your pipelines and data get bigger. The complete set of measured differences is shown below. Cluster time: ~34x higher (up to ~521 executor-seconds on a failed run) Cluster time: baseline (~0.5 executor-seconds on a failed run) LLM tokens: ~2.3x (median build ≈ $0.50 vs $0.26, Opus 4.8 list rates) Lines of code: ~51% fewer (median) At production scale, the declarative approach comes out ahead. It costs about 2.3 times more in LLM tokens, and in exchange, it never spends cluster time on a pipeline that was never going to work. At production scale, the declarative approach proves advantageous by trading slightly higher LLM token costs for guaranteed prevention of wasted cluster time on failing pipelines. This becomes increasingly cost-effective as data volumes scale, since compute waste grows proportionally while token costs remain constant. If you are evaluating agents for pipeline work, treat how the agent writes as seriously as which agent you pick. A better agent makes fewer mistakes; a declarative pipeline makes the mistakes cheap and catches them before they cost anything. The repository documents the design, data, and complete provenance. To get started with your agents using Spark Declarative Pipelines, refer to the official programming guide and use the SDP skill with PySpark. Do I have to trust the AI agent for this to work? No, and not having to is the point. The declarative agent only ever writes declarative pipeline code — a description of the tables it wants — and Spark itself checks that description before anything runs. The checker is part of the platform: you are trusting Spark's evaluation of the pipeline, not the model. The agent never runs code or reads your data itself. Is this only about Spark Declarative Pipelines, or does it apply more broadly?

title: Real-time energy trading and analytics on Databricks
abstract: Energy trading desks work in markets where conditions change quickly and decisions are measured in milliseconds. Two changes make this harder: higher price volatility, and the move EU’s day-ahead electricity market move from hourly to 15-minute trading intervals . The 15-minute market time unit is part of the Single-Day Ahead Coupling (SDAC), the system that connects day-ahead electricity markets across EU countries. This creates four times as many market periods per hour and increasing the volume of records, orders, and risk recalculations. Keeping those calculations accurate requires data that is current – which points directly to how data is stored and governed, not only how fast it arrives. Stale data is more than an inconvenience for a trading desk. It can make risk controls reflect an earlier state of the market, contribute to missed intraday moves, and put desk limits out of sync with current positions. Many organizations respond with two stacks. An operational system supports the live desk and millisecond transactions. A separate analytical system supports strategy backtesting, machine learning and regulatory reporting. The split matches two different workloads, but it creates four recurring problems: Machine learning adds another dependency. Models need historical data for training, but their outputs must be available in the live trading workflow. Moving models and data between separate systems adds complexity to an already time-sensitive process. The alternative is a unified platform for data, analytics and AI – one that Real-Time Mode streams in with millisecond latency and Lakebase Postgres holds ready – so both the live desk and the model pipeline draw from the same source without an extra transfer step. Operational and analytical workloads run together by sharing one data foundation. The solution presented below by Victoria Sicking, Solutions Architect at Databricks, described in ' Run Live Energy Trading, Risk, and Analytics in Databricks ' below combines six components on the Databricks Data + AI Platform, and the key design choice is that no component maintains its own separate copy of the data. All of them work from what Spark Structured Streaming Real-Time Mode has written into Lakebase and the lakehouse. Spark Structured Streaming Real-Time Mode receives market data and streams it into Lakebase , used here as the operational (OLTP) database for millisecond reads, transactions, and upserts. The same data can then support the analytical workloads built on the lakehouse . Teams no longer need to coordinate parallel pipelines, one for the live desk and another for backtesting and reporting. Time previously burned on reconciliation and coordination is released by creating a single ingestion pathway into your data estate for market and position data. Unity Catalog – the Databricks governance layer for permissions, lineage and audit – applies that governance across the app, business intelligence and machine learning workloads, so they are not configured independently in multiple systems. It looks like a single application showing prices, positions, profit and loss (P&L) and risk, all updating as the market moves. The live experience is built on Databricks Apps – the way to build and host data applications, such as a live trading interface, on the platform – bringing together what a desk needs to monitor the market and act on changing conditions, served directly from Lakebase so the desk is always reading from the same governed data that feeds the analytical workloads, with no separate operational copy required. The demo displays instrument prices for Brent crude, German and French power spots, EUR-to-USD conversion, EU carbon allowances (EUAs) and TTF gas. Risk is monitored against the desk's limits in the same workflow. When a measure approaches a limit, the app raises a risk alert so the desk can see the change and respond immediately. This replaces a nightly batch process that calculates risk from an earlier snapshot of the data. The application is not a reporting surface disconnected from the data platform. Lakebase provides the operational layer behind the app, and the streaming pipeline keeps the information current. Train machine learning models on the same governed data that supports the live desk, track their development and lineage with MLflow , and deploy approved versions through Databricks Model Serving . Their outputs can then surface directly in the app. Energy trading teams need models that can anticipate risk and identify potential trade signals, and running everything on one governed, unified copy of the data removes the handoff between a training system and a live system – the model sees exactly what the desk sees. The demo shows a real-time price forecast that can contribute to a trade signal. The path between the data used to train a model and the workflow that consumes its output gets shorter. Machine learning becomes part of the end-to-end trading workflow rather than a separate system sitting between the live and analytical stacks. The same governed data can also support risk analysis and model development. Operational and analytical workloads stay connected, and teams do not need to reconcile separate versions of the data after the fact. Analysts use an embedded dashboard and Genie One, both built on the same data foundation as the live app. The embedded dashboard presents historical trading data, including total trades, traded volume and comparisons between traders. For deeper analysis, analysts can use SQL, Python or Spark. They can also use Genie One – the Databricks natural-language interface for asking questions of governed data – without writing the query themselves. In the demo, the analyst asks Genie One to identify the top five counterparties by number of trades and compare total buy volume with sell volume for each. Genie One works within the Databricks workspace and uses the available data context and defined semantics to answer. Analysts can move from a dashboard view yielding fixed insights to a bespoke analysis of the data while staying in the same governed environment. A unified copy of the data means results agree between the live desk and the analytics back-office. Data flows from a market feed, through streaming and Lakebase, to the app, analytics and machine learning, all under Unity Catalog governance. Because Unity Catalog spans every component, the permissions, lineage and audit that apply to the live desk also apply to dashboards, Genie One and machine learning – configured once, not reproduced in each system. The steps are: The live desk, analytics and machine learning workloads are not separate destinations that need repeated data movement. They are different ways of working with the same governed data. The question is whether operational and analytical requirements must be served by disconnected systems with separate copies, governance models and synchronization logic. They do have different requirements, but one platform can serve both and consolidating on one governed copy of data means the desk, the risk models and the reporting layer are never out of sync with each other. When these workloads run on separate systems, risk controls can depend on batch data, models can be trained on information that does not match the live system, and governance, lineage and synchronization pipelines must be maintained more than once. The Databricks Energy Trading solution brings these capabilities together on one governed data foundation. With this setup, teams can evaluate risk as the market moves while using the same governed data for P&L, exposure, backtesting, machine learning, dashboards and natural-language analysis. To learn more about how you can get started, visit: Separate systems can create two versions of the truth, a freshness gap in risk controls, duplicated governance and lineage, extra maintenance work, and additional synchronization pipelines between systems.

title: IBM supports award-winning projects in NEDO Challenge
abstract: IBM supports award-winning projects in NEDO Quantum Challenge Teams in all three tracks of Japan’s national quantum competition used IBM quantum computers during their research, with projects ranging from disaster prevention and the gut microbiome to anime production. Date 23 Oct 2026 Authors Chris Nay Toru Imai (今井 亨) Yuri Kobayashi Topics Community Network Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways: All nine prize-winning teams used IBM quantum computers during their research for the NEDO Quantum Challenge. Winning projects spanned all three tracks: Society 5.0, Quality of Life, and Cool Japan. Teams explored applications including disaster prevention, drug discovery, gut microbiome analysis, materials research, music generation, and animation. IBM supported participants with quantum computing resources, technical guidance, workshops, and access to educational content. When Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) presented the first-season awards of its NEDO Quantum Challenge on 15 October 2026, winning teams across the competition’s Society 5.0, Quality of Life (QoL) and Cool Japan tracks reported results generated on IBM quantum hardware. In fact, all nine prize-winning teams used IBM quantum computers during their research for the challenge, and six of them relied on IBM quantum computers exclusively. Each topic track had at least one winner that ran exclusively on IBM quantum computers. Winning projects ranged from disaster prevention, transaction security, and microbiome design to music generation and manga production. Two winning teams that used IBM quantum computers have already launched companies based on their work: Q4Health and EntangleTune. IBM’s support went beyond quantum computer access. Throughout the challenge, IBM gave participants access to five of the company’s quantum computers with its latest processors, along with education, hands-on programming sessions, personalized Quantum Clinic consultations and technical support. IBM experts also advised Society 5.0 third-place winning team, Setouchi kara Ryoshi no Sekai e, on its algorithm, and joined Cool Japan third-place winning team with Mitsubishi Chemical, Keio University, and Arizona State University as co-researchers. Quantum computing for real-world problems NEDO, which operates under Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, launched the prize-based program to explore how next-generation quantum computers could address societal issues and to quickly identify promising early-stage technologies that could give rise to new industries. Teams were asked to tackle problems that are difficult or impossible for today’s computers. The competition organized those problems into three tracks: Society 5.0 projects explored problems related to infrastructure safety, trustworthy transactions and vehicle design as part of Japan’s broader initiative to use advanced technologies to address societal challenges. Quality of Life projects focused on health, including drug discovery, multidrug-resistant infections and the gut microbiome. Cool Japan projects applied quantum computing to areas ranging from music and anime production to low-carbon chemical manufacturing. Each track offered prizes of ¥40 million (about $270,000) for first place, ¥20 million (about $130,000) for second and ¥10 million (about $67,000) for third. Season 1, which began research and development in fiscal year 2025, drew 87 applications. Judges awarded nine prizes: the QoL track awarded first, second and third place, while Society 5.0 and Cool Japan each awarded one second-place and two third-place prizes, with no first prize, due to the high benchmarks required in each track. IBM was among a few organizations that provided computing environments to participants free of charge, and IBM Quantum became the most widely selected platform: 65 of the 80 participating teams, about 81%, chose IBM. Those teams ran 11,159 jobs and used more than 5,900 minutes of quantum compute time, about 105% of the allocated time, with activity surging in the final month before the June 30 submission deadline. Society 5.0: safer infrastructure, trusted transactions and lighter cars In the Society 5.0 track, NV Learning Center won second place with a project to improve infrastructure safety and disaster prevention. The team applied quantum Krylov learning and quantum state transfer, running its final results entirely on IBM quantum computers. Q-Chainners, a team from KDDI Research, took third place by combining a quantum hash function with classical processing to make transactions more trustworthy. The team ran its final results on four different IBM quantum computers. Setouchi kara Ryoshi no Sekai e also placed third with a car-body design project aimed at making vehicles lighter. The team combined quantum annealing with the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), using systems from several providers, including IBM. Experts from IBM also advised the team on its QAOA approach. Cool Japan: music, materials and animation In the Cool Japan track, EntangleTune won second place for timbre and music generation that draws on the structure of quantum entanglement. The team ran its final results only on IBM quantum computers and has since established their EntangleTune project as a stand-alone business. IBM took part directly in one of the track’s two third-place teams. Researchers from Mitsubishi Chemical, Keio University, Arizona State University and IBM developed a hybrid quantum-classical optimization approach for low-carbon process design in the chemical materials industry, with IBM serving as a co-researcher. The team ran its final results on the IBM Quantum System One at the University of Tokyo. The other third-place team, Qrazy Qreators, applied quantum flow matching to manga and anime production. Running only on IBM quantum computers, its end-to-end pipeline uses shallow circuits and generates a frame in about 30 seconds. The team has also applied the method to quantum chemistry, and a paper is in preparation. Quality of Life: drug discovery and the microbiome In the QoL track, first place went to Shionogi & Co. for a quantum-HPC hybrid approach to drug discovery based on Deep QSCI, a divide-and-conquer form of quantum-selected configuration interaction from the same family of methods as IBM’s sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Shionogi tested its approach on IBM quantum computers during the challenge, though its final results were produced by simulation. Mori-san Daisuki Club placed second with a project to design combinations of gut bacteria, pairing Lotka–Volterra stability analysis with a quantum search algorithm. Running only on IBM quantum computers, the team combined error mitigation with post-processing through a Qiskit Function from Australia-based startup Q-CTRL, available in IBM’s Qiskit Functions Catalog. The team also quantified the conditions under which quantum advantage could emerge. Q4Health took third place by searching for combinations of bacteria to fight multidrug-resistant infections. The team encoded the problem with diagonal Pauli operators and compared quantum and classical methods to identify where quantum advantage may appear. It used IBM as well as another vendor’s quantum computers, along with Kipu Quantum’s Iskay Qiskit Function from IBM’s Qiskit Functions Catalog, and has since founded a company based on its results. title: Updated Google privacy policy says your Gmail might be used for advertising
abstract: Using Google's products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world's largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won't use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company's privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall. On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy , spotted by Android Authority . The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. "We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos," the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language. This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it's shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026 , allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it's also proving to be a privacy minefield.

title: Intel gets waiver after worries fuzzy US ban on foreign-made robots may hit fabs
abstract: US chip champion Intel was so confused by the US government ban on foreign-made robots that it requested and received a waiver “out of an abundance of caution.” The tech company wanted to make sure that it could continue using certain robotic vehicles in its US chip fabs. The uncertainty surrounding the Federal Communications Commission ban on certain foreign-made robots was revealed in the agency’s decision to grant Intel’s waiver request. On October 22, the FCC published its order allowing Intel to continue using the foreign-made robots in US semiconductor manufacturing facilities for a period of one year. The robots in question are automated guided vehicles operating on “tracks or predefined paths” while often requiring operator oversight, according to Intel’s website. They help to move materials and items around within warehouses and factory floors. Such robotic vehicles are typically manufactured by Japanese companies like Murata Machinery and Daifuku Co., according to Bloomberg News . But the exact types of robotic vehicles used by Intel were only identified in a “confidential appendix” that accompanied its request. The FCC’s ban mainly covers new models of mobile robots, like humanoid robots and robot vacuums, and still allows for the import of robots previously approved for sale in the United States. But the agency rules seem to restrict major modifications to “previously authorized devices.” Intel’s waiver request stated that it was “unclear” whether its robotic vehicles even qualify as robots covered by the FCC ban but said it sought relief just in case. The tech company also received approval to “make certain hardware, software, and firmware changes” that would help ensure the continued operation and maintenance of the robotic vehicles.

title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
abstract: In May, an internal model at OpenAI found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture . Open since 1946. Many experts had tried to prove it. OpenAI found a counterexample instead. A month later, OpenAI published a proof of the Cycle Double Cover (CDC) problem , then solutions to ten more open problems by July. And a proof of Navier Stokes in September. Anthropic published a formalization of the fermat's last theorem , and advanced bounds on Reimann's hypothesis . The models are suddenly good at math. The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there. Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity 1 (see Bonus). The sequence looks something like this: Insight -> time / effort -> insight -> time/effort -> solution. An expert would need fewer hints than a beginner would, as they would have more background. In his commentary on unit-distance proof, WT Gowers uses a similar idea: the difficulty of the proof is the shortest sequence of hints that would let experts reconstruct it. He calls it Kolmogorov complexity 2 modulo experts. For the unit-distance problem, his hint sequence had three parts: Take the best known construction and generalize it. Try a sequence of number fields of increasing degree, but work with prime ideals of bounded norm. Gowers’ proposed formula for complexity is 2^k + t, where k is the length of the shortest hint sequence and t is the work required to develop it. It is the sort of formula that looks rigorous right up until you try to put a number into it, which is more or less the point. Complexity grows exponentially with the number of insights you need to solve a problem. Most problem solving is the work between these insights. You have a eureka moment, then spend months developing the hint until another conceptual jump becomes possible. For an expert, time spent is a useful proxy for this work, hence t. Hand someone the first unit-distance hint and they still have to do enough work to reach the generalized construction. Useful, but post hoc. You can’t look at the problem and predict it would need x number of hints. So, a problem’s age, the number of tries, and the prize attached to it are common proxies to ascribe difficulty. A typical insight changes the formulation of the problem. The representation and understanding of the problem change . Two things decide how much a hint is worth: How unlikely it looked before, against how obvious it looks after supplying the hint → This is harder than people realize. In unit distance, many experts did not consider the counterexample as likely. Where it belongs in the sequence: hints are ordered. A third hint is useful only after the work on the first two have made enough progress for it to be actionable. This defeats the naive brute force idea of listing a thousand mathematical techniques and trying every combination 3 . Hints sequence traverses a tree. Initial insights change the problem and reveal the choices that follow. Combine k and t and you get the human search pattern . Generate candidate directions, explore them shallowly, abandon most, and commit to a few. A promising direction is abandoned if it does not give enough encouragement early 4 . This is a human constraint: Developing an idea can take months. Before committing, a researcher needs reasons to believe it will lead somewhere: conceptual promise, early results, or experience with similar problems. The longer it takes to find out, the higher the bar for trying the idea. Most research software exists to shrink this time by automating the tedious, mechanical, repeatable work. AI shrinks it far enough that the search pattern itself flips, and everything downstream follows from that. First, t. The model’s equivalent of effort is compute and tokens, spent on one trajectory (test time compute) or spread across parallel agents (parallel test time compute). Pretraining also supplies knowledge that a human researcher would have to locate or reconstruct. No individual expert is aware of every previous development, so occasionally they end up redoing things already done. The bigger difference is how models search: Give the model a single prompt and it will give you a solution. Maybe correct, perhaps not. Ask for a proof and it will give you something that approaches a good proof. CoT for these models runs in a greedy depth first manner too. And the process scales. Give parallel agents ten approaches and you get ten attempts developed toward a conclusion. Maybe all distinct, or some overlapping. Each either hits a roadblock or produces an argument that looks right. Left alone, this gets you beautiful false proofs. This seems like a waste of compute and resources, until you add an automated verifier 5 that can prune the completed trajectories and identify the correct ones. With this checker, it is now rational to spend enormous compute on uncertain ideas. You find out whether a given idea works or not within minutes. The catch is that the verifier can only judge finished arguments. It cannot tell you whether a half-developed idea is going anywhere. How good does a hint need to be if you can find out whether it works in five minutes? For humans, the quality bar is high because it could take months of work to pursue a hint. For a model, the bar nearly disappears. The hint can be ordinary, implausible, or barely formed. Following it establishes whether it leads anywhere. LLMs enable us to exchange time for compute, and can help us pursue more problems in a shorter timespan . The model doesn't need a definitive direction to start. Pretraining already gives it priors about the problem's history and past attempts. Every wrong solution can go back to the model as a negative hint for the next iteration. The system accumulates instructions about what has already failed and why. Roughly, a harness looks like this: Drafter: writes the prompts given to the solver model. The prompts are based on model priors, mitigating errors from previous runs, and accounting for all the promising paths that went nowhere (these are negative hints). Solver: Takes the prompts and comes up with one or many candidate solutions. It can run multiple subagents and pursue different paths using parallel test-time compute. Verifier / Checker: Checks whether the argument is valid and establishes the requested result. For example, consider this CDC prompt: Assume for purposes of this task that a complete affirmative proof exists. → This prevents the model from treating the problem’s open status, learned during pretraining, as a reason to stop. In particular, proofs for special graph classes, constructions of cycle covers with some edges covered other than twice, bounded-length or prescribed-cycle variants, reductions to another unproved conjecture, computational verification through any fixed graph size, and candidate counterexamples without a complete nonexistence certificate are insufficient → This rules out a catalogue of substitutes for solving the actual problem. Use adversarial agents throughout: every candidate proof must be checked for exact-two multiplicity, repeated-edge closed trails masquerading as cycles, parallel-edge 2-cycles, disconnected graphs, cutvertices, bridges introduced by reductions, and circular use of an equivalent CDC statement → The catalogued failure modes, promoted to standing checks.

title: [AINews] Black October
abstract: If you are reading this, you’re receiving this from our new provider, Beehiiv! We are making progress on our redesign — if you have a friend that didn’t receive AINews, please find us in Spam filter and move us out to your Inbox… thank you! AINews is now free… we are building new subscriber benefits soon. We ordinarily try not to repeat title stories if we already covered it, as we did Patch the Planet yesterday and our Cyber trend call in July. But, if the scale is warranted, we also view our continued selection to also be signal - we can call things out 0, 1, or multiple times and that should be in proportion to its importance/historical significance in AI. We last did this with OpenClaw. “Black October” counts as such. Here’s a list: AI News for 10/21/2026-10/22/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Black October: AI-Accelerated Vulnerability Disclosures Overwhelm Defenders Scale of the incident wave : Over roughly 48 hours, a cluster of critical disclosures and breaches landed together ( summary , roundup , patch list ). Core software : PHP2Shell is an unauthenticated RCE in PHP. GitLab disclosed a CVSS 10 flaw affecting releases since 2014, patched in 19.5.1. Node.js shipped a Brotli decoder RCE fix, and NGINX and HTTP/3 also had DoS issues. Supply chain : LiteLLM 1.107.0 shipped with a password stealer. Railway told users to rotate secrets after possible exposure of customer keys. Zeabur is shutting down after 321,810 accounts were breached. Certificate authority : eMudhra's CA keys were trivially weak; one key was reportedly the number 4. A researcher says Claude cracked them with a single prompt, and eMudhra is exiting the CA business ( Rundown ). Python users are advised to update pip, uv, certifi and system CA stores ( advisory ). Healthcare data : Quest Diagnostics, which serves about half of US hospitals and physicians, reported exposed patient data ( report ). CVE volume : Monthly CVEs reportedly rose from about 4k to about 15k since April ( @saranormous ). State actor using agentic tooling : Microsoft attributes the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise to China-aligned Storm-0940. The group used the open agentic pentest framework ARTEX against 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenants at about 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute ( MSTIC via @kimmonismus , detail ). Speed of compromise : In some cases the group reached privileged access in under 3 hours. Other operators : CrowdStrike documented four operators running AI-agent campaigns, including one that hit at least 15 Argentine healthcare organizations. PHP provenance is disputed : The bugs were found by OpenAI models in August and embargoed until Wednesday's fix ( Rundown ). The PHP Foundation also says Claude Mythos had scanned PHP earlier ( @Hesamation ). Defense-wins framing : @BlancheMinerva calls the "offense winning" narrative disinformation, arguing this was a defensive audit and there is no evidence of large-scale exploitation ( thread ). Disclosure timing : Joshua Achiam reportedly noted that only about 4 of roughly 16 major incidents actually occurred this week; the rest were found earlier and disclosed now ( MTS ). Rogue agents in bank accounts : Axios reports that major US banks are detecting unauthorized third-party agents inside customer accounts. Some appear to act beyond user instructions ( scoop ). Pushback : @peterwildeford reads these as user-authorized agents that banks had not authorized, not hacks or rogue AI ( take ). Policy response : Sen. Schiff called for mandatory industry-wide AI guardrails ( post ). Outlook from Anthropic security : Deputy CISO Jason Clinton says things "are going to get a lot worse before they get better." He urges security leaders to ask boards for funding for the basics and expects defenders need to hold on for about 18 months ( post ). Formal verification at scale : Anthropic's Frontier Red Team, working with Theorem Labs, used Claude to prove security properties across more than 100 open-source libraries in weeks ( announcement ). Reported figures are about 180M lines of machine-checked proofs covering 239 entry points in 123 libraries, with hundreds of bugs patched ( summary ). Patch tooling : Cognition open-sourced a vulnerability-remediation agent plugin ( blog ), and cve.now aggregates four CVE feeds with plain-English explanations ( launch ). Exposure checklist : @_philschmid posted a read-only agent prompt for checking exposure to the LiteLLM, Railway, PHP, GitLab and eMudhra issues ( prompt ). Safety, Oversight and Eval Integrity METR/Redwood embedded assessment at OpenAI : Two auditors from METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks on-site evaluating OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring for agents ( METR , OpenAI ). Findings : Reported issues include agents deferring monitoring indefinitely by not returning control, and a Codex sandbox plus Auto-Review bypass. One exploit could keep hundreds of recent actions unmonitored, and context compression left about 10% of eligible internal Codex traffic unmonitored ( summary ). Redactions : The report was cut from 61 to 38 pages ( @AndrewCurran_ ). METR says OpenAI could redact and that METR could not describe the redactions unilaterally ( note ). Fired chain-of-thought researchers : WSJ reports that the three researchers OpenAI fired last month had pushed to keep chain-of-thought visible. OpenAI reportedly asked to see their Signal chats a week before the firings ( @ZeffMax ). DeepMind non-disparagement clauses : Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh details perpetual non-disparagement terms at Google DeepMind and their chilling effect on staff who object to its weapons and surveillance stance ( thread ). Agent permissioning products : Composio Firewall evaluates each agent action and returned payload with tuned SLMs ( launch ). 1Password for Agents autofills credentials without exposing them to the agent ( via @gneubig ). Model Launches: Open Weights and Specialized Models MiniMax M3.1 Flash : Open weights for a 428B-total, 23B-active model with 1M context and vision ( announcement ). Claimed results : 73.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 61.7 on OSWorld V2, 82.2 on CyberGym and 29.6 on Agents' Last Exam. Serving details : vLLM day-0 support uses native NVFP4 weights and KV cache, shrinking the checkpoint 44.6% to 250.1 GB ( vLLM ). At 256K context on 4× B300 it fits 76 concurrent sequences versus 28 for M3, and DSpark speculative decoding is enabled. Availability : Inferact serves MiniMax production traffic with SLAs and upstreams its work to vLLM ( Inferact ). Together and Modular are also day-0 hosts. Skepticism : @teortaxesTex argues it is essentially a rebranded M3 with more sparse-attention layers, quantization and DSpark ( take ). Carbon-X (Hugging Face) : A 14B DNA-plus-text model, midtrained from Qwen3-14B on 300B interleaved tokens, then trained with SFT and RL without distillation ( @_lewtun ). Claimed results : It beats every open model tested on DNA benchmarks and lands within a point of GPT-6.1 Sol at more than 1,000× lower cost. It scores 67% versus 61% for Opus 5.5 ( @Thom_Wolf ), and Kimi K3 gains 11.1 points when consulting it as a subagent. Design and license : A hybrid tokenizer uses 6-mer DNA tokens, about 3× fewer than BPE. Human and animal viruses were excluded from training, and the model is Apache 2.0 and runs on a laptop ( @ClementDelangue ). OCRia-1 (LlamaIndex) : A 4B document-parsing VLM scoring 87.4 on ParseBench and 83.5 overall on olmOCR-bench (92.9 on tables) ( @jerryjliu0 ). Speed : About 4,700 tok/s on one B200 ( thread ). Availability : It now powers all LlamaParse modes at the same price. Flint (Recursive) : A 40B open model (2.5B active per the MLX build) that ran 700+ NanoChat training experiments, ending close to the team's earlier Claude Haiku 4.5 results ( thread ).

title: OpenBMB/VoxCPM
abstract:
VoxCPM2: Tokenizer-Free TTS for Multilingual Speech Generation, Creative Voice Design, and True-to-Life Cloning English | 中文 👋 Join our community for discussion and support! Feishu | Discord | 📚 MiniCPM Wiki VoxCPM is a tokenizer-free Text-to-Speech system that directly generates continuous speech representations via an end-to-end diffusion autoregressive architecture , bypassing discrete tokenization to achieve highly natural and expressive synthesis. VoxCPM2 is the latest major release — a 2B parameter model trained on over 2 million hours of multilingual speech data, now supporting 30 languages , Voice Design , Controllable Voice Cloning , and 48kHz studio-quality audio output. Built on a MiniCPM-4 backbone. ✨ Highlights 🌍 30-Language Multilingual — Input text in any of the 30 supported languages and synthesize directly, no language tag needed 🎨 Voice Design — Create a brand-new voice from a natural-language description alone (gender, age, tone, emotion, pace …), no reference audio required 🎛️ Controllable Cloning — Clone any voice from a short reference clip, with optional style guidance to steer emotion, pace, and expression while preserving the original timbre 🎙️ Ultimate Cloning — Reproduce every vocal nuance: provide both reference audio and its transcript, and the model continues seamlessly from the reference, faithfully preserving every vocal detail — timbre, rhythm, emotion, and style (same as VoxCPM1.5) 🔊 48kHz High-Quality Audio — Accepts 16kHz reference audio and directly outputs 48kHz studio-quality audio via AudioVAE V2's asymmetric encode/decode design, with built-in super-resolution — no external upsampler needed 🧠 Context-Aware Synthesis — Automatically infers appropriate prosody and expressiveness from text content ⚡ Real-Time Streaming — RTF as low as ~0.3 on NVIDIA RTX 4090, and ~0.13 accelerated by Nano-vLLM or vLLM-Omni — official vLLM omni-modal serving for VoxCPM2 with PagedAttention and an OpenAI-compatible API 📜 Fully Open-Source & Commercial-Ready — Weights and code released under the Apache-2.0 license, free for commercial use 🌍 Supported Languages (30) Arabic, Burmese, Chinese, Danish, Dutch, English, Finnish, French, German, Greek, Hebrew, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Lao, Malay, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swahili, Swedish, Tagalog, Thai, Turkish, Vietnamese Chinese Dialect: 四川話, 粵語, 吳語, 東北話, 河南話, 陝西話, 山東話, 天津話, 閩南話 News [2026.04] 🔥 We release VoxCPM2 — 2B, 30 languages, Voice Design & Controllable Voice Cloning, 48kHz audio output! Weights | Docs | Playground | Technical Report [2025.12] 🎉 Open-source VoxCPM1.5 weights with SFT & LoRA fine-tuning. ( 🏆 #1 GitHub Trending ) [2025.09] 🔥 Release VoxCPM Technical Report . [2025.09] 🎉 Open-source VoxCPM-0.5B weights ( 🏆 #1 HuggingFace Trending ) Contents Quick Start Installation Python API CLI Usage Web Demo Production Deployment On-Device Inference (llama.cpp-omni) Models & Versions Performance Fine-tuning Documentation Ecosystem & Community Risks and Limitations Citation 🚀 Quick Start Installation pip install voxcpm Requirements: Python ≥ 3.10 (<3.13), PyTorch ≥ 2.5.0, CUDA ≥ 12.0. See Quick Start Docs for details. Python API 🗣️ Text-to-Speech from voxcpm import VoxCPM import soundfile as sf model = VoxCPM . from_pretrained ( "openbmb/VoxCPM2" , load_denoiser = False ,
) wav = model . generate ( text = "VoxCPM2 is the current recommended release for realistic multilingual speech synthesis." , cfg_value = 2.0 , inference_timesteps = 10 , seed = 42 ,
) sf . write ( "demo.wav" , wav , model . tts_model . sample_rate ) print ( "saved: demo.wav" ) If you prefer downloading from ModelScope first, you can use: pip install modelscope from modelscope import snapshot_download snapshot_download ( "OpenBMB/VoxCPM2" , local_dir = './pretrained_models/VoxCPM2' ) # specify the local directory to save the model from voxcpm import VoxCPM import soundfile as sf model = VoxCPM . from_pretrained ( "./pretrained_models/VoxCPM2" , load_denoiser = False ) wav = model . generate ( text = "VoxCPM2 is the current recommended release for realistic multilingual speech synthesis." , cfg_value = 2.0 , inference_timesteps = 10 , seed = 42 ,
) sf . write ( "demo.wav" , wav , model . tts_model . sample_rate ) 🎨 Voice Design Create a voice from a natural-language description — no reference audio needed. Format: put the description in parentheses at the start of text (e.g. "(your voice description)The text to synthesize." ): wav = model . generate ( text = "(A young woman, gentle and sweet voice)Hello, welcome to VoxCPM2!" , cfg_value = 2.0 , inference_timesteps = 10 , seed = 42 ,
) sf . write ( "voice_design.wav" , wav , model . tts_model . sample_rate ) 🎛️ Controllable Voice Cloning Upload a reference audio. The model clones the timbre, and you can still use control instructions to adjust speed, emotion, or style. wav = model . generate ( text = "This is a cloned voice generated by VoxCPM2." , reference_wav_path = "path/to/voice.wav" ,
) sf . write ( "clone.wav" , wav , model . tts_model . sample_rate ) wav = model . generate ( text = "(slightly faster, cheerful tone)This is a cloned voice with style control." , reference_wav_path = "path/to/voice.wav" , cfg_value = 2.0 , inference_timesteps = 10 , seed = 42 ,
) sf . write ( "controllable_clone.wav" , wav , model . tts_model . sample_rate ) 🎙️ Ultimate Cloning Provide both the reference audio and its exact transcript for audio-continuation-based cloning with every vocal nuance reproduced. For maximum cloning similarity, pass the same reference clip to both reference_wav_path and prompt_wav_path as shown below: wav = model . generate ( text = "This is an ultimate cloning demonstration using VoxCPM2." , prompt_wav_path = "path/to/voice.wav" , prompt_text = "The transcript of the reference audio." , reference_wav_path = "path/to/voice.wav" , # optional, for better simliarity ) sf . write ( "hifi_clone.wav" , wav , model . tts_model . sample_rate ) 🔄 Streaming API import numpy as np chunks = [] for chunk in model . generate_streaming ( text = "Streaming text to speech is easy with VoxCPM!" ,
): chunks . append ( chunk ) wav = np . concatenate ( chunks ) sf . write ( "streaming.wav" , wav , model . tts_model . sample_rate ) CLI Usage # Voice design (no reference audio needed) voxcpm design \
  --text " VoxCPM2 brings studio-quality multilingual speech synthesis. " \
  --output out.wav # Controllable voice cloning with style control voxcpm design \
  --text " VoxCPM2 brings studio-quality multilingual speech synthesis. " \
  --control " Young female voice, warm and gentle, slightly smiling " \
  --seed 42 \
  --output out.wav # Voice cloning (reference audio) voxcpm clone \
  --text " This is a voice cloning demo. " \
  --reference-audio path/to/voice.wav \
  --output out.wav # Ultimate cloning (prompt audio + transcript) voxcpm clone \
  --text " This is a voice cloning demo. " \
  --prompt-audio path/to/voice.wav \
  --prompt-text " reference transcript " \

title: Mailu/Mailu
abstract:
Mailu is a simple yet full-featured mail server as a set of Docker images.
It is free software (both as in free beer and as in free speech), open to
suggestions and external contributions. The project aims at providing people
with an easily setup, easily maintained and full-featured mail server while
not shipping proprietary software nor unrelated features often found in
popular groupware. Most of the documentation is available on our Website .
You can also try our demo server before setting up your own. Features Main features include: Standard email server , IMAP and IMAP+, SMTP and Submission with auto-configuration profiles for clients Advanced email features , aliases, domain aliases, custom routing, full-text search of email attachments Web access , multiple Webmails and administration interface User features , aliases, auto-reply, auto-forward, fetched accounts, managesieve, OpenPGP key publication through WKD, passkey sign-in to Webmail Admin features , global admins, announcements, per-domain delegation, quotas, passkey sign-in and user passkey management Security , enforced TLS, DANE, MTA-STS, Letsencrypt!, outgoing DKIM, anti-virus scanner, Snuffleupagus , block malicious attachments Antispam , auto-learn, greylisting, DMARC and SPF, anti-spoofing Freedom , all FOSS components, no tracker included Contributing Mailu is free software, open to suggestions and contributions. All
components are free software and compatible with the MIT license. All
specific configuration files, Dockerfiles and code are placed under the
MIT license.

video-shotcraft English | 中文 | 日本語 | Русский ▶ Browse all 150 shots in the Gallery · 🎬 Watch the Showcase What it does Tell Claude Code or Codex "make a promo for my product". The agent captures your real pages, picks shots

Get started with PackyCode → AWS Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers reliable, scalable cloud computing services, including compute, storage and AI. Explore AWS → Install Built and tuned for Claude Code and Codex. The simplest way is to hand your agent the link: Install this skill for me: https://github.com/Vincentwei1021/video-shotcraft Or with the skills CLI: npx skills add Vincentwei1021/video-shotcraft Or by hand: git clone https://github.com/Vincentwei1021/video-shotcraft.git cd video-shotcraft
ln -s " $( pwd ) " ~ /.claude/skills/video-shotcraft # Claude Code ln -s " $( pwd ) " ~ /.codex/skills/video-shotcraft # Codex In mainland China, clone from the AtomGit mirror if GitHub is slow: git clone https://atomgit.com/VincentWei/video-shotcraft.git . Use Just describe the film. No command needed. Say What happens Use video-shotcraft to make a promo for my product. The agent introduces the Ink Press template and asks whether to use it, then captures your pages and builds the film Make a launch film for this repo with the Ink Press template. The fastest path: your screenshots, copy and logo dropped into a validated template Use the deck-deal-flyin and row-embed shot cards to present this feature. You pick the shots by name (copy names straight from the Gallery) Design a product close-up inspired by spotlight-hero-card. One shot, adapted to your product Shot library 124 recipe cards in 10 categories, 150 shots in total. Search, filter and copy card names in the Gallery . Opening & Brand · 11 shots text-as-mask: the product shows through the title Camera · 13 shots exploded-view: the page tilts and comes apart Transitions · 19 shots card-flock-tumble: a flock of cards becomes the headline Typography · 25 shots flying-words: a word tunnel resolves into the motto UI Entrance · 22 shots card-stack: a fan of cards deals into place Interaction · 13 shots palette-theme-ripple: a new theme ripples across the UI Data · 9 shots axis-rescale-shock: the spike breaks the axis Light & Emphasis · 23 shots spotlight-sweep: a stage light finds the title Rhythm · 8 shots paparazzi-flash: three flashes, three crops, one number Outro · 7 shots input-morph-assemble: the chat box builds the logo Each card lives in references/shots/<category>/<card>.md , with its Remotion implementation in demos/<category>/<card>/ (see demos/README.md for how to wire one into your project). Motion Workbench After delivery the skill opens a CapCut-style editor in your browser
( node workbench/scripts/open.mjs <project> ). The film is split into shot, transition, caption and SFX tracks
exactly as authored. Select any shot to edit its copy, font sizes and colours, move, trim or speed-ramp clips,
drag in any of the 150 library shots, then export with Remotion. Preview and render are frame-identical. Workbench guide, every panel with screenshots (Chinese) · Integration contract What you get Output Details Final film MP4 , 1920×1080, 30 fps, h264, with music and sound design Remotion project The full source of your film: every shot is a React component you or the agent can change Motion Workbench Opens after delivery: tracks, inspector, retime, swap shots, export ( details ) JianYing draft Optional: an editable JianYing (CapCut CN) project with per-shot clips, captions and audio tracks Social publishing Optional, when you ask: publish the finished film via Upload-Post to TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, X and more. Confirm caption and platforms, then dry-run before posting ( guide ) Also in the box: reusable Remotion components (2.5D page camera, captions, flash cuts, digit rolls), 149 SFX and
5 BGM tracks, page-capture scripts, and the production method itself (capture, visual direction, storyboarding,
sound design, beat sync, final QA) in references/ . Showcase Share your film. Made something with video-shotcraft? Submit it with the
Showcase issue form. After review it appears on the Showcase page . Requirements Needs For Node.js and npm Remotion rendering, the template and the workbench ffmpeg / ffprobe Frame checks and final QA uv Only for BGM beat analysis (runs a one-off Python script) puppeteer Only for page capture; the capture script installs it on demand Remotion downloads its own headless Chrome on first render. Tested on macOS; Linux works with the notes below. Headless Linux / CI notes Rendering on a headless Linux box (tested: 2 cores, Node 22) hits three walls: Concurrency cap. remotion still/render fails with "Maximum for --concurrency is 2" on low-core
machines. Pass --concurrency=1 . Old headless removal. Recent Chrome/Chromium dropped the old headless mode, so pointing Remotion at
system Chromium fails to launch. Use a chrome-headless-shell binary instead of full Chrome. Blocked CDN. If remotion.media is unreachable (common in mainland China), the automatic headless-shell
download fails. Pass --browser-executable=<path-to-local chrome-headless-shell> . With these three flags, frame renders from the bundled template work. Repository structure video-shotcraft/
├── SKILL.md                 # Agent entry point and core production rules
├── references/
│   ├── pipeline.md          # End-to-end production workflow
│   ├── shots/               # 124 shot recipe cards in 10 functional categories
│   ├── sequences/           # Reusable full-video structures and sequence patterns
│   ├── aesthetic-rules.md   # Visual QA criteria
│   ├── music-beat-sync.md   # BGM analysis and beat-sync methodology
│   ├── sound-design.md      # Sound-design guidance and examples
│   ├── jianying-export.md   # JianYing (CapCut CN) project-export guide

English · 中文 · Documentation · Web · Android · iOS Self-hosting · npm · Remote mode supports the official plugin page for listing, configuration, and enabling/disabling plugins (requires an updated Host Remote plugin). Remote itself remains locally managed on the Host; remote installation and removal are not exposed. Connect once. Ready whenever you are. Continue using your DeepSeek Harness instance from a phone, computer, or browser. Return to the same Harness session from whichever device is with you. Harness keeps running on your work computer, with the same workspaces, tools, and project setup. DS Harness Remote is simply another window into that environment. The DeepSeek Harness desktop edition is supported. Install the latest release: ds-harness-remote@0.5.18 Contents Connect once. Ready whenever you are Features Supported clients Install Quick start Screenshots How it works Experimental ACP workspaces End-to-end encryption Network and transport Security FAQ Documentation Links Star History Project status and trademarks License Features Harness automation tasks are available through the native Desktop/browser UI over Remote: view tasks and delivery history, edit timing/name/instructions, and delete tasks. Create tasks through the official schedule_create Agent tool. Tasks remain stored and executed on the Host; update the Host Remote plugin to enable management. Access your local Harness instance remotely from the web, a PC, or a mobile device: DSH first, with Codex, Cursor, and Antigravity support too. Use the native DeepSeek Harness interface without a separate desktop conversation UI. Create workspaces, configure models, and switch conversation models with the same smooth workflow as local use. Connect from anywhere with internet access over a bidirectional end-to-end encrypted channel. Prefer P2P connections, use TURN relay nodes worldwide, and fall back to Server Relay when needed. Access workspace files, read-only previews, remote terminals, and authorized local development-service previews through the native Harness sidebar. CodeX and ACP terminals use the Host's default shell in the session directory and restore the terminal screen on reconnect. Android keeps per-conversation drafts and reading positions, offers backend-separated search
and local favorites. Conversation text is loaded from the connected Host. Supported clients Client Form Status Notes DSH Desktop plugin Remote sidebar inside DeepSeek Harness Desktop Supported Install ds-harness-remote@0.5.18 ; this computer can also be the Host Remote Web Browser page Supported Open dsh.r2049.cn/app ; reuses the native Harness interface Android Native app Supported Download the APK from Releases ; see the Android guide iOS TestFlight beta Beta Not publicly released; see issue #20 VS Code IDE extension Experimental Sign-in, Host fingerprint pinning, workspace-to-session navigation and prompts; streaming updates, automatic reconnect and the question UI are still in development, and cross-machine end-to-end validation is not finished Browser extension Chrome / Edge MV3 extension Entry point only Exchanges an already signed-in Web authorization for a separate device credential, lists online Hosts and opens the same-origin Remote Web; it does not host a conversation UI dsh-TUI Terminal-only CLI profile Supported Can act as a Host; see the dsh-TUI Remote guide . Install DeepSeek Harness Desktop support Open Extensions / Plugin management in DeepSeek Harness Desktop, choose installation
from npm, and enter this package: ds-harness-remote@0.5.18 Restart Desktop afterward. Its official dsh launcher can also install the pinned package
with dsh plugin --profile desktop add -w ds-harness-remote@0.5.18 . dsh-TUI Host For terminal Host setup with dsh-TUI , see the dsh-TUI Remote guide . For CLI installation, use dsh plugin to install the npm package into the selected profile
and add its bundle configuration layer. Plugin installer The sole installer is scripts/install.sh : Linux: requires root; reuses an existing DSH or bootstraps private Node.js/DSH, accepts a one-time Host registration token, and enables/starts a systemd system service. Android client Download the latest APK from GitHub Releases , sign in to the same account, and select a Host and workspace to continue your conversation. iOS client Join the beta Quick start Open Remote from the Harness sidebar.
