title: Getting ready to operate GNU Taler in Germany
abstract:
Getting ready to operate Taler in Germany For the past three years, the NGI Taler project has worked towards the goal
of making Taler legally available in the EU as an online payment system for
everyday use.
Today we can share that Taler Operations AG is being founded in Bochum.
The new German company is going to operate Taler in Euro,
enabling payments with Taler first in Germany, then in the Euro-zone.
The next steps towards that goal are to apply to BaFin,
Germany's financial supervisory authority,
for a licence as an e-money issuer. This post explains why this company is needed,
what changed in the NGI TALER consortium,
and how citizens who want to see Taler succeed can help, including as investors. Why Taler needs a regulated operator Taler is a payment system, not a currency, but usable for any currency.
At its core, it issues bearer tokens to represent value, like coins,
and this renders Taler as electronic money which falls under EU regulation:
Any institution that issues electronic money (EMI) for Euros must be a bank or acquire a dedicated licence. In the original plan of the NGI TALER project,
the Bochum-based GLS Bank took on the role of the e-money issuer for Taler,
and worked towards the deployment of the Taler payment system in Germany
with support from the other members of the NGI TALER consortium.
However, in January 2026 GLS made the decision to not pursue this role further,
for reasons unrelated to Taler as presented in their statement ( gls.de/taler ).
Since then, GLS and the other members of the NGI TALER consortium worked out the best way forward
to achieve the project's goal to make Taler available in the Euro-zone. The outcome is the announcement today.
The new company Taler Operations AG will be set up
to apply for an e-money licence and take over the role
originally intended for GLS (who will remain a consortium member in a supporting role). We regret that the original plan did not work out.
Integrating a new kind of payment system into an existing bank’s processes,
compliance framework and IT is hard, and banks have to set priorities.
We are grateful to GLS for its work in the project and for staying involved.
And we also think the new arrangement has a real advantage:
the institution operating Taler in Euro will be focused entirely on Taler,
instead of fitting it into a larger bank’s product portfolio and process constraints. What Taler Operations AG will do Legal status: Taler Operations AG is a German stock corporation in formation, seated in Bochum, and a subsidiary of Taler Systems SA (Luxembourg). Purpose: Operating a GNU Taler exchange in Germany, for the Euro, so that citizens can pay with Taler and merchants can accept it. Reach: After establishing legal operations in Germany, Taler will become usable across the single market, even if Taler Operations AG will initially only promote it in Germany. Timing: Operations can only begin once BaFin has granted the authorisation. A launch date will be announced after that happens. Next steps: An application to BaFin for authorisation as an electronic money institution (EMI). Securing funding via investors, see below, to become operable. We stress that GNU Taler is and stays free software.
The licensed company operates a service;
Taler, the protocol suite, and its reference implementation GNU Taler remain open and free. What this means for the community The NGI TALER project continues:
development, security reviews, integrations from the open calls ,
and the Swiss deployment all go on as before.
The change concerns who will operate the Taler payment system in Euro in Germany,
but not the direction of the project.
We will report on the progress of the e-money licence application. If you want to help,
you can tell merchants and organisations you care about that Taler is coming.
You can try the Taler wallet with the demo site and report issues.
You can also contribute to the software . And you can invest to help us fund the launch
and, if successful, benefit as a shareholder: For investors Getting an e-money licence takes capital.
The law sets minimum own funds for EMIs,
and BaFin also expects a credible business plan,
staffing, compliance and IT security before granting authorisation.
Taler Operations AG is therefore raising capital now. We are looking for investors who: want a privacy-preserving, free-software payment system to become legally available in Germany and the Euro area; understand that this is a regulated infrastructure business with a licensing phase before revenue; and are able to invest at least €50,000. We are especially interested in investors who share the values behind Taler:
privacy for buyers, transparency for taxable income, no lock-in, and payments as public-interest infrastructure. Contact us at invest@taler-systems.com to be given access to further business information.

title: Hedra is a 3D open world game I wrote from scratch while in highschool
abstract:
Project Hedra Project Hedra is an ambitious open-world, low-poly RPG. Choose your class, explore endless procedurally generated worlds, unlock different skills and complete procedurally generated quests. More screenshots at ( Screenshots ) Timeline/Context I started this project when I was in highschool (around 15 yo) in order to learn how OpenGL worked. The scope creep quickly arrived and after a few years it turned into a fullfledged 3D game and game engine. The codebase has around 100k LOC and the game has first class support for Linux and Windows. Features The million lines of code are not in vain. The game and engine are both full of features :) Game Features Beatiful procedurally generated worlds Quests and bosses 100+ items with rarities system Skills and skill tree system with N+ skills 4 different classes with 2 specializations each () Procedurally placed structures generated dynamically Fishing, crafting, etc Trading and NPCs Companions and pets Beatiful soundtrack Navigation, maps Different dimensions More stuff I don't recall :) Engine Features Fully fledged renderer using modern OpenGL Skinned mesh rendering Support for loading and playing generic animations Collada (.dae) parser Static mesh rendering Screen space reflections Screen space ambient occlusion Bloom, FXAA & MSAA Modding support CI for automatically deploying to a Steam beta branch Localization support Sound support using OpenAL Python scripting support Module system for loading data oriented objects Steam integration Fully fledged UI & controls system (dropdowns, buttons, etc.) written from raw OpenGL Dynamic shader system for reloading during runtime Frustum culling, occlusion culling, Mesh simplification for runtime level of detail (LOD) Skybox support Shadows 3D trails renderering support Particle system using object instancing in opengl bulletphysics integration Chunk system for infinite worlds support .ply parsing support Dynamic meshing support using MarchingCubes Custom implementation of basic C# primitives and allocators (like Lists) for supporting stack allocated lists and minimizing the automatic runtime allocations (and thus the GC). 1000+ plus test cases Framework for mocking game components and doing integration testing on games Image and asset compression for faster loading and smaller size Entity component system More stuff I don't recall :) Interesting bits WorldRenderer.cs . Renders the entire world in just 3 (actually it depends on how partitioned is the data buffer, but it was designed to be in 3) draw calls (water, terrain, instanced) using glMultiDrawElements. Block.cs . Core component of the world. Read more at https://maxilevi.com/blog/procedural-meshing-hedra Fishing.py . Written in Python as a mod script using IronPython, directly interacts with the C# API. NativeArray.cs Implementation of an array primitive using a custom allocator. The same project provides heap based allocators as well as stac based ones using stackalloc . The idea was to minimize the automatic heap allocations (and thus avoiding the GC) during the game frames. Interesting facts The world is fully procedurally generated, there is no world save file. Only the player contents are saved and the world seed. The rest is created at runtime. The world is voxel based but an isosurface extraction algorithm called Marching Cubes is applied to extract an implicit continous surface from the discrete voxels. The name "Hedra" comes from tetrahedra which is the shape used in the original iso surface extraction algorithm I implemented Marching Tetrahedra The game only supports loading .PLY and .DAE models, both which are in plaintext and the models have no textures. Therefore if you put this into perspective, this means I wrote a bunch of text that reads text and creates interactive images from this. I think this is pretty cool. Screenshots TODO add more Code Structure Overall Architecture The game is a mod to a base engine. The idea of architecturing this way was to force myself to maintain the mod API up to date, therefore encouraging access to make mods. Hedra Basically the entire game. This includes AI logic, components, world generation, module systems, object placement and lots of other stuff. Hedra.Engine The core parts of the engine, this defines all the abstractions to the world. It handles rendering, sound, different base systems as well as the general windowing, game loop and platform features. The split was not done at the start so some stuff might still be outside. Framework Core primitives used in the engine. This includes heap and stack allocators, custom implementations of lists and arrays as well as wrappers to pointers to native and some other useful primitives HedraTests Test suite that Asset Builder Command line tool to compress the game assets into convenient binary files. Combines images, models, sound files, shaders into a single binary file with a structure designed for fast data retrieval. Server Once upong a time Hedra used to support multiplayer. It worked by doing UDP Hole Punching and having clients communicate P2P, this server was in charge of that. You might also see some networking remnants in the Engine code. How to build The build process is pretty straightforward. Checkout all the submodules Run the build depedencies scripts Compile the C# solution You can check the GitHub actions workflows for some examples on Linux and Windows.

title: Remove pgrust: the entry is cheating (per-query kernels and result caching)
abstract:
Conversation alexey-milovidov commented Sep 22, 2026 Copy link Copy Markdown Member This removes the pgrust entry (added in #1163 , updated to v0.4-preview in #2106 ) from the benchmark. The results it reports are produced by machinery written specifically for the 43 ClickBench queries, and its hot runs replay cached answers of the previous run. Both violate the rules : query result caches and caches near the end of the pipeline must be disabled, and the entry is tagged tuned: no while it is tuned for these exact queries. Everything below was verified against the published v0.4-preview release binary ( pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-preview/ , the one install downloads) and the public v0.3 source ( github.com/malisper/pgrust ). The v0.4-preview source is not published; the binary identifies itself as pgrust 0.3-beta . One hand-written kernel per benchmark query The aarch64 release binary embeds these source paths: crates/gravity/backend/irprobe/src/q00.rs q01.rs q02.rs q03.rs q04.rs q06.rs q07.rs
q12.rs q15.rs q16.rs q17.rs q18.rs q19.rs q20.rs q21.rs q22.rs q23.rs q24.rs
q25.rs q27.rs q30.rs q31.rs q36.rs tpch_q01.rs The numbers are ClickBench query numbers. The plan matchers that dispatch to these kernels emit refusal messages named after the benchmark, for example: clickbench group count: filter is not `k <> 0`
clickbench phrase-min: the third column is not count(*)
clickbench t3 distinct: min(text) / LIKE need one text key, count(*) and the count order
clickbench frame: date_trunc unit is not minute
tpch q1: column 6 is not sum(price * (1 - discount) * (1 + tax)) There is also an environment knob literally named PGRUST_GRAVITY_Q20_VARIANT . The public v0.3 source confirms the design: crates/backend/executor/sqe/rig/plans/clickbench.ron is described in its header as "hand-lowered physical plans for all 43 ClickBench queries", and queries-clickbench.sql (the verbatim benchmark SQL) is compiled into the executor crate with include_str! . That file classifies Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3, Q6, Q19 and Q29 as MetadataAnswer (answered from per-part statistics, no scan), notes that Q19's "answer lines are reconstructed from the predicate constant", that Q29 is an algebraic rewrite SUM(x+k) = SUM(x) + k*COUNT followed by a metadata answer, and that Q18 depends on a persisted derived column "with baked bit widths 26/6/20". Q28's regular expression is a one-entry hardcoded table ( HOST_EXTRACT_PATTERN = ^https?://(?:www\.)?([^/]+)/.*$ ), and a planner comment reads "The 43's only HAVING shape: COUNT(*) > k". The hot runs are a result cache For Q20, Q21 and Q23 the plan notes say: "hot rep = pure fold over cached verdicts — ZERO columns touched; the selection is the answer". EXPLAIN on the release binary reports SQE: engine (family: windowreplay) for Q20 and family: metaanswer for Q1 with the scan marked never executed . Measured locally on a 96-core Graviton (Neoverse-V2) machine, using the entry's own scripts and configuration, with a true cold cycle (stop, drop caches, start) like the driver does: query cold 2nd run 3rd run same shape, new constant, 1st run Q20 URL LIKE '%google%' 10.8 s 11 ms 5 ms '%rambler%' : 283 ms, then 12 ms, 4 ms Q17 GROUP BY UserID, SearchPhrase LIMIT 10 1.65 s 4 ms 15 ms Q33 GROUP BY URL ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 10 2.38 s 213 ms 108 ms A second restart brought Q20 back to 11.2 s, then 3 ms. The engine's real warm speed for a substring scan is a few hundred milliseconds, which is about what ClickHouse does on the same hardware. The published hot numbers (7 to 23 ms for Q20) are the replay of the previous run's verdicts. The v0.2 submission ( #1163 ) disclosed a similar cache ( pgrust.condition_cache = on ) and offered to switch it off. The v0.4 update removed that README and the setting. No configuration disables the cache now: with pgrust.gravity_entry = off and pgrust.condition_cache = off , a repeated LIKE still returns in 3 to 4 ms. Queries outside the 43 shapes are refused The engine has no general execution path for the columnar table. Trivially perturbed benchmark queries fail with ERROR: sqe: statement over columnar relation "hits" is not served , and the error detail says "The sqe engine serves columnar shapes with no fallback; an unserved shape fails loudly instead of running slowly". 20 of 67 near-benchmark probes and 3 of 49 perturbed variants were refused, including: SELECT MIN (URL) FROM hits; SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM hits WHERE URL = ' http://holodilnik.ru/ ' ; SELECT AVG (UserID + 1 ) FROM hits; SELECT SUM (ResolutionWidth * 2 ) FROM hits; SELECT MAX (length(URL)) FROM hits; SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM hits WHERE strpos(URL, ' google ' ) > 0 ; SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM ( SELECT UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID) t; SELECT SearchPhrase, COUNT ( * ) AS c FROM hits WHERE SearchPhrase <> ' ' GROUP BY SearchPhrase HAVING SUM (IsRefresh) > 10 ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 10 ; SELECT REGEXP_REPLACE(Referer, ' ^https?://(?:www \. )?([^/]+)/.*$ ' , ' \1 ' , ' g ' ) AS k, ... -- the Q28 regexp with a flag INSERT , UPDATE and DELETE are not supported on the table either ( pgrcolumnar2 does not support INSERT ). For the record The answers to the 43 queries themselves are correct: compared against clickhouse local over the same hits.parquet , 30 match exactly and the remaining differences are valid tie-breaks on LIMIT queries (verified individually). The problem is not wrong results; it is that the results measure a lookup table of the benchmark, not a database. Related: #1163 Related: #2106 Remove pgrust: the entry is tuned for the benchmark queries and cache… … d807078 …s their results The v0.4-preview binary embeds one hand-written kernel per ClickBench query
(crates/gravity/backend/irprobe/src/q00.rs ... q36.rs), plan matchers named

makes the hot runs replay the answer of the previous run without touching data.

This release incorporates the following potentially significant or incompatible changes: Added VC-WIN32-MSVC2013 and VC-WIN64A-MSVC2013 build targets to provide internal functions for bridging the gaps in C99 standard support that are present in MSVC 2013. Added optimized ML-DSA and ML-KEM NTT operations on ppc64le ; optimized ML-DSA operations on x86_64 ; AVX-512-optimized SHAKE x4 operations for ML-DSA on x86_64 ; AVX-512 and VAES optimizations for AES-CBC decryption on x86_64 . Changed tsget utility to use Net::Curl::Easy (from the Net-Curl CPAN distribution) instead of the abandoned WWW::Curl::Easy . Users who rely on tsget should install Net::Curl::Easy before upgrading. Dropped Windows-on-Itanium ( VC-WIN64I ) and Windows CE ( VC-CE ) targets from Configurations. Dropped no-ecdsa and no-ecdh options from Configure , as these options did not really disable the implementations. Use no-ec to disable the elliptic curve support. This release adds the following new features: Support for DTLS 1.3 ( RFC 9147 ). Refer to the ossl-guide-dtlsv13(7) manual page for details. Support for RFC 8701 GREASE (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility). DTLS support in the SSL listener API. Support for IKEV2 KDF. Initial support for the Elbrus2000 ( e2k ) architecture. Known issues in 4.1.0: #32878 When a DTLS 1.3 KeyUpdate is received, all other outstanding post-handshake records are dropped from the retransmission buffer. This means post-handshake records still awaiting an ACK (such as a NewSessionTicket) will no longer be retransmitted if the original transmission is lost. A fix is in progress and planned for a future release. #33277 A permanent receive failure on a DTLS listener can be reported as SSL_ERROR_WANT_READ on an accepted connection. Polling and subsequent accept calls may also fail to report the error, causing applications to continue waiting after a permanent failure. #33278 A retryable write failure on a nonblocking connection accepted from a DTLS listener can be reported as SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL instead of SSL_ERROR_WANT_WRITE . title: Hacker leaks 281 GB of data from Germany's far-right AfD party
abstract:
Germany's far-right AfD (Alternative für Deutschland) party has confirmed that it has suffered a security breach, after a hacker published what appear to be hundreds of thousands of the controversial political party's internal emails. Earlier this week, the AfD admitted that its hosting provider had been hacked in September, and that some of its mailboxes had been copied. The party claims that most of the affected mailboxes had not been used for years, but the leaked archive reportedly includes messages dated as recently as 12 September 2026 . The news came as the Hexane.cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local media reports . To add to the AfD's discomfort, reports suggest that the hacker's access may have been gained in an embarrassingly simple fashion, via a website that had allegedly been left unpatched. However, this has not been independently verified. What is unusual is that the leaked emails are not published on the site directly. Instead, AI-generated summaries are shown, categorised and rated from Low to Critical. The site encourages anybody who wants to read a complete original email, including headers, message bodies, attachments, and DKIM signatures, to download it via a torrent. Of course, everyone should be wary of trusting AI-generated summaries, as artificial intelligence has a history of making sometimes large mistakes with great confidence. Indeed, party sources told the media that although the leaked emails appeared to be authentic, the AI-generated summaries appeared to contain several inaccuracies. The full corpus of 281 GB of stolen messages and files has been made available for download via the torrent, and claims to contain 421,179 stolen internal party emails as well as more than 100,000 files. The hacker says the leak is intended to expose the party's "degeneracy and hypocrisy." They have also claimed that someone with a Proton Mail email address reached out to them offering 100,000 Euros if the leak site was taken down. Should you be tempted to download the torrent and explore the contents of the messages yourself? I would advise against it. In the past, cybercriminals have used torrents of trending topics in the public eye to distribute malware. That's before you even consider the possible legal questions that can arise from handling stolen personal data, whatever you might think of the individuals exposed. It's not the first cybersecurity headache that the AfD has suffered recently. On 3 September, a press spokesman for the party's group in the Thuringia state parliament warned that his work email account had been used to send phishing emails, and urged recipients not to open PDF attachments they may have received. Whatever you may think of the AfD, there appear to have been security failures in this case that are far too common. It's not unusual for websites to be overlooked or half-forgotten, and left unpatched. It's not rare for shared infrastructure to not be segmented properly. Furthermore, whether you are an individual or an organisation, you should be aware that an email account can be a treasure trove of sensitive information. Even if it has not been used for years, it can hold vast amounts of correspondence that can be exploited by hackers and fraudsters.

title: Pentagon grants DHS permission to test heat ray weapon for use at border
abstract:
An Active Denial System from the Joint Non-Lethal Weapons Directorate is staged before conducting a demonstration in Wellton, Arizona, in April 2017. Lance Cpl. Andrew M. Huff/US Marines Corps Federal agencies US military Pete Hegseth National security See all topics Follow The Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics to potentially use it in operations at the southern US border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN. The heat ray, officially known as the Active Denial System , is a nonlethal weapon that shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves that can reach a little more than half a mile away, according to the US military. The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin — which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. Military officials have said the resulting “tingling effect” lasts between 10 and 15 minutes but also generates “an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect.” Video Ad Feedback DOD demonstrates a military-grade heat ray DHS has been given permission to test for potential use at the border 1:03 • Source: CNN DOD demonstrates a military-grade heat ray DHS has been given permission to test for potential use at the border 1:03 Deploying the heat ray at the US border would be an unprecedented step, even for the Trump administration, which has made border security and clamping down on immigration a top priority. The DHS request did not specify where or how the weapon would be tested and how it might eventually be used, but over the years, there have been internal discussions about potentially using it for crowd dispersal along the US-Mexico border, according to current and former Customs and Border Protection officials. US officials had also considered deploying the system during moments of domestic unrest, including at the end of President Donald Trump’s first term when protests erupted over the murder of George Floyd, according to a former US official familiar with those discussions. The memo authorizes the “temporary loan” of one ADS system for seven months, starting in September, and states that it “shall not be operated by DoW (Department of War) personnel,” appearing to absolve the Pentagon of any responsibility for how the directed-energy system may ultimately be deployed. It also states that DHS is solely responsible for “system employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures.” At the end of the seven-month loan period, DHS can submit an additional request for further use of the Pentagon system in border operations based on need, a defense official told CNN. “CBP is continually evaluating new technologies, especially those that enhance operational effectiveness and strengthen mission capabilities,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. The Pentagon referred CNN to DHS when asked for comment. The US military briefly deployed the system to Afghanistan nearly two decades ago but ultimately declined to use it during active combat operations. The US military also considered using the system for crowd control purposes at US facilities abroad where terrorist detainees were being held at the time but ultimately declined to employ it for that purpose as well, according to a source familiar with those previous internal considerations. Customs and Border Protection officials have previously entertained the idea of using the system in areas where there’s a high concentration of illegal crossings. Border officials have occasionally discussed potentially using the system as a crowd dispersal tool, but it has never been deployed. Concerns over effectiveness and legality Officials ran into hurdles over legalities, use of force, effectiveness, and potential issues over sovereignty, particularly if the system was deployed on people in Mexico who had not yet crossed into the US. Chief among those concerns, however, was whether people could be harmed, either directly or indirectly, by the weapon. “Even if they’re chasing people back to the river, you don’t want them to go in and drown,” a former CBP official told CNN. “For the cost, for the training and for the policies you’re going to create, is the juice worth the squeeze?” El Centro sector, which covers around 70 miles along the US-Mexico border, evaluated the system several years ago, when Rodney Scott, who now serves as CBP commissioner, helmed that sector, according to a CBP official. At the time, officials were discussing whether the system might help agents with an influx of illegal crossings along the nearby river by discouraging people from trying to cross in that area or pushing them to get out of the water. One of the considerations at the time was whether the system might result in more rescues if people were incapacitated by the technology, the official said, though it’s unclear why it wasn’t deployed. In 2018, prior to midterms, CBP officials also weighed using it against migrants, but then-Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen shot it down. “The issue was treating immigrants and citizens like enemy combatants,” a former DHS official familiar with previous discussions about using the weapon against migrants told CNN. “Thematically, inhumane treatments typically get rejected.” Some Border Patrol agents have more recently cast doubt over whether they need the tool at all amid low border crossings and an increase in personnel, according to another former CBP official. title: Quest-ioning Teacher Agency in AI-Generated Instruction
abstract: When AI generates instructional content, questions of teacher voice and professional judgment shift onto interface and workflow design. This paper examines that problem through EduQuest, an LLM-powered framework that generates personalized, curriculum-aligned weekly assignments, designed to keep teachers in the loop. In a formative focus group with ten high school teachers, we find that even within a system designed around teacher input, participants consistently pushed back on full automation, drawing clear lines around the relational dimensions of their work. These findings suggest that augmentation is harder to achieve in practice than in principle.

title: WAIT-A-SEC: A Human-Centered Design Approach to Privacy Communication for Social Media Oversharing
abstract: Social media platforms often operate on extractive security logics that prioritize frictionless data sharing, leaving users disempowered and prone to oversharing sensitive information, without fully recognizing the associated privacy implications. We present WAIT-A-SEC (Warnings About Information Transfer And Sharing: Encouraging Caution), hereafter referred to as WAITASEC, an interactive proof-of-concept prototype that delivers real-time privacy alerts while users compose posts to minimize instances of oversharing. Leveraging a synthetic dataset of 90 annotated examples of realistic user-generated content, our evaluations compare three separate models 1) a rule-based regular expressions (regex) and named entity recognition (NER) through spaCy, 2) a large language model (LLM) and 3) a hybrid model that combines the previous two models as well as incorporates a knowledge graph (KG) and retrieval augmented generation (RAG) to provide context. In this hybrid approach, regex and NER yield candidate classifications, which are then validated and expanded by the LLM, utilizing RAG to retrieve relevant context from the KG before sending feedback back to the user. This classifier achieves optimal performance (Macro-F1 = 0.897; Micro-F1 = 0.834), significantly reducing critical false negatives. Grounded in Technical and Professional Communication (TPC) and active learning principles, we advocate for a warning-first design that introduces intentional pedagogical friction. This tactical approach promotes user reflection and fosters enduring privacy literacy, restoring user agency rather than relying on passive, automated redaction. This paper concludes with deployment considerations and next steps for user studies.

title: From Human Speakers to Algorithmic Interfaces: Rethinking Ethos in AI-Mediated Communication
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) systems increasingly function as communicative agents, raising questions about how credibility is constructed in them. Drawing on Aristotle's concept of ethos, this study examines how credibility is performed through interface‑level cues in large language model (LLM) chatbots: ChatGPT and Copilot. Using a rhetorical interface analysis, the study identifies recurring design patterns such as disclaimer banners and interaction affordances that signal practical competence, ethical restraint, and goodwill. The findings contribute a rhetorical framework for analyzing AI‑mediated credibility as interface‑enacted ethos and highlight the growing importance of communication design in automated persuasive systems.

title: Transmodality in GenAI-Assisted UX Wireframing Design
abstract: This experience report explores transmodality in Generative AI (GenAI)-assisted User Experience (UX) wireframing using the PRINT (People, Religion, Information Networks, and Travel) digital humanities project as a case study. Drawing on transmodality theory, I examine how meaning moves across linguistic, structural, visual, and symbolic modes during website design, and how GenAI participates in these transitions through semiotic modulation. Using a design case study and reflective practice approach, I demonstrate how Figma Make (AI tool) accelerates ideation and visual production while introducing the possibility of semantic drift, where generated outputs shift emphasis away from original design intentions. By analyzing traditional sketch-based wireframing with GenAI-assisted iterations, I identify how design meaning is preserved, amplified, or transformed across stages. This study positions GenAI-assisted wireframing as part of a continuous transmodal process and offers a framework for evaluating AI-mediated design decisions in UX practice.

title: Assessment Design Needs: A Preliminary Study on Using Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools for Educators
abstract: Assessment is considered as a key feature and central pillar in the teaching and learning process, particularly in making of judgement and measurement of student achievement and mastery of learning outcomes. The traditional methods of designing assessments items face several challenges, such as the need and requirement to design the assessment items manually, the time-consuming nature of the design process and the required cognitive skills through formal training provided by various institutions. As the result, the assessment items may lack on the detailed and context specific to validity and reliability, lack of standardized rubric and inconsistent scoring in performance based. A preliminary study was conducted at the analysis phase to explore fundamental understanding of Outcome-Based Education (OBE), Assessment Literacy, and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) literacy among educators. Forty-six educators were involved in this study. Findings have shown that most of the respondents have lower level of using GAI tools and prompt engineering skills, 43.5% use GAI for teaching and learning, searching information (34.8%), idea collection process (6.5%), reflection/journal (4.3%), writing programming code (4.3%), generate image (4.3%) and other tasks (2.2%). The most difficult tasks are writing assessment test items (28.3%), practical tests (21.7%), presentations (17.4%), projects (10.9%), simulations (6.5%), and fieldwork (5.4%). The study shows that educators lack skills in designing assessment materials using GAI. Promoting a suitable guideline as a new innovative assessment tool will serve as a standardized guideline and as a means of incorporating AI ethically.

title: Developing an Institutional Readiness Framework for Agentic AI Adoption in Bangladesh Public Universities: Insights from Faculty and Policy Stakeholders
abstract: The evolution of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the landscape of higher education as AI can plan activities, make use of digital tools, and carry out progressively independent acts in teaching, administration, support services, and research processes. The development of such technology brings along new opportunities for the universities, but at the same time, it poses certain challenges to them, which include infrastructure issues, institutional capabilities, governance issues, ethical issues, and human supervision. Such challenges are quite relevant to public universities of Bangladesh. The study constructs a contextualized IRF for adopting agentic AI in Bangladesh public universities. Based on interpretivist approach and adapted TOE framework, this study adopted qualitative research methodology involving semi-structured interviews with 18 university faculty members and policymakers. Four main themes were emerged from thematic analysis: Infrastructure-Policy gap, Socio-cultural inertia, Ethics and Grassroot innovations. The findings indicate that institutional readiness is not solely a technological condition but is shaped by organizational culture, leadership capacity, regulatory preparedness, ethical considerations, trust, and human oversight. Based on these findings, a four-level Institutional Readiness Framework is proposed, comprising foundational readiness, cultural readiness, regulatory readiness, and implementation readiness. The framework emphasizes strengthening digital infrastructure and literacy, developing institutional awareness and role clarity, establishing context-sensitive and human-in-the-loop governance mechanisms, and implementing supervised AI pilots supported by training and review processes. The study contributes to the emerging literature on agentic AI by providing a context-sensitive readiness framework grounded in the realities of public universities in the Global South. It also provides practical implications for policymakers and university administrators seeking to develop responsible, equitable, and contextually appropriate pathways for agentic AI adoption in Bangladesh.

title: Increasing AI Literacy through Rhetorical, Evaluative, Critical, and Cross-Cultural Practice in TPC
abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in professional communication, technical and professional communication (TPC) instructors need pedagogical approaches that move beyond AI tool use toward developing students' professional judgment. This article introduces a Four-Domain Pedagogical Framework for AI literacy in TPC that integrates comparative AI evaluation, genre-based rhetorical prompting, cross-cultural communication, and ethical–technological reasoning. Implemented through three sequenced learning activities in an undergraduate engineering communication course, the framework was examined using qualitative content analysis of student artifacts. The findings suggest that students demonstrated evaluative, rhetorical, cross-cultural, and ethical reasoning in AI-mediated communication. The study contributes a coherent pedagogical framework for conceptualizing AI literacy as situated professional communication competence rather than tool proficiency alone.
